I wish to direct the attention of the government to this very important question. In the session of 1901 a deputation waited upon the hon. the Minister of Customs and drew his attention to the fact that very uneven tariff conditions existed between Canada and the United States, in so far as farm and market-garden products were concerned, and the hon. the leader of the opposition moved a resolution during that session which reads as follows :
This House regarding the operation of the present, tariff as unsatisfactory, is of'opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at all times secure the Canadian market for Canadians.
And that the financial policy of the government should include a measure for the thorough and judicious readjustment of the tariff at the present session.
It was thought that the government would do something for the farmers and market-gardeners in the session of 1901.
1 do not think that any government ever had a better opportunity to do something for so important a class, because the resolution 1 have just read declared the opinion of the hon. leader of the opposition and his followers upon that question. With this expression of policy on the part of the leader of the opposition and his supporters, the government could have had a resolution adopted unanimously giving to the farmers and market-gardeners the protection they are entitled to. However, in the session of 1901 that resolution was voted down. The hon. leader of the opposition and his supporters recorded their votes in favour of better protection to the farmers and market-gardeners and the right hon. gentleman and his supporters voted down that resolution, so that a distinct issue between the two parties was created on that subject. The Liberal-Conservative party voted in favour of protection and the right bon. gentleman and his supporters opposed better protection to the farmers and market-gardeners. Nothing was done in the session of 1901, and in the session of 1902 another deputation waited on the hon. the Minister of Finance. A very large and influential deputation was received from the province of Ontario and Quebec and submitted resolutions for consideration by that bon. minister and bis colleagues-resolutions which had been passed by the Farmers and Market-Gardeners Association of Quebec and Ontario. This large and influential deputation pointed out to the minister that something should be done for the farmers and market-gardeners if they were to retain the Canadian market. During that session the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) moved this resolution :	[DOT]
j That it is greatly in the interests of the | market-gardeners and the farmers that the ; duties on our Canadian garden products be i raised so as to give an effective protection against foreign competition.
That resolution expressed the policy of the opposition in this House, but when it was submitted to a vote, the right hon. the leader of the government and his followers voted it down. In the session of 1903, the hon. member for Laval again introduced the same resolution, and important speeches were made pressing some very important facts on the attention of the government, showing that a large quantity of market and farm products was being imported into this country, coming directly into competition with the products of our farms and gardens. It was pointed out also that the present tariff does not give any special advantage because under tlie ad valorem system of duties, very large quantities of goods were brought in under value, so that there was practically no protection whatever to the interests of the farmers and market-gardeners. This, Sir, is an important question, and I wish to place upon record the one-sided tariff that exists between Canada and the United States. The United States tariff is 45 cents per bushel on beans. Canadian tariff is 15 cents, the United States tariff is 25 cents per bushel on potatoes ; the Canadian is 15 cents. On apples the American tariff is 75 cents per barrel and the Canadian 40 cents. On onions the American tariff is 40 cents per bushel, and the Canadian 25 per cent ad valorem. Cabbages, under the American tariff, are charged 3 cents per head, and under the Canadian 25 per cent ad valorem.
You will see, Sir, by this short list that the duties are entirely in favour of the United States farmer as against the Canadian, and what our resolution asks is that the Canadian tariff shall be made equal to the American. Would you allow me to give an example of how this one-sided tariff works out ? Last year we imported for home consumption from the United States $228,640 of potatoes and we exported but $50,969 worth.

That is the amount we have imported from the United States of these articles, coming in direct competition with similar products of the Canadian farmer. There was a time when it was said that we in Canada could not produce all these articles. Indeed, in the discussion of last session and the session before, some lion, gentlemen on the other side ventured to say that we could not produce many of these articles that we were importing into Canada, or that we could not produce them early enough in the sea-son, when there was a certain demand among the richer classes in Canada for them. But the conditions are constantly changing. There was a time in the history of this country-and not so many years ago-when it was thought that we could not produce roses, when it was thought that, if we required cut flowers in our larger cities, we had to import them from the United States. But (things are entirely changed owing to the thrift of the Canadian people ; and, in the town in which I have the honour to live, there is a large rose-growing industry covering thirteen acres with grass ; and last year this company, the Dale Estate, which is so well managed by Mr. Duggan and Mr. Algie. produce more than $100,000 worth of cut flowers and these were sold from one end of Canada to the other while some small proportion, I am glad to say was exported to the United States. During this session a gentleman from Manitoba gave his evidence before the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization. I refer to Mr. A. P. Stevenson, a prominent Manitoban. As to fruit-growing in that province, Mr. Stevenson pointed out that, not many years ago it was thought impossible to produce apples in Manitoba : but the farmers there have faced this fruit problem and now there is some portion of the apples used in Manitoba that are produced in that province. And he ventured to say that, in a very short time, all the apples required for home consumption in Manitoba could be produced by the Manitoba farmers themselves. That should set at rest the question whether Canada Mr. BLAIN.
can produce the articles which we are now importing from the United States. This is an important consideration and one that, I am sure, will appeal to the intelligence of the government when they are discussing their policy upon this subject.
I wish now to point out the very large quantity of certain fruits that are being imported into Canada under the free list. For instance, I find that in 1893 we imported into Canada 430,240 bunches of bananas, while, last year, 1903, we imported 942,443 bunches, or an increase in ten years in the importation of bananas alone of 512,203 bunches. To show how rapidly the consumption of this fruit is increasing in Canada I may point out that the importation in 1902 was 705.707 bunches. Thus, with an importation of 942,443 bunches last year, we find that in one year there has been an increase in this import of 176.076 bunches. Then I take the item of pineapples. In 1893. we imported 010,031, while in 1903, we imported 1,375,220. In 1902 our importation of pineapples was 1,095,949, so that there was an increase last year of 279.277. I do not wish to be misunderstood on this question. We have no special complaint at this moment with respect to the importation of these articles. These articles, as is well understood, are not grown in Canada.

I do not say that the farmers or market-gardeners have any complaint on this question, but I do say that the great free list in our customs law will require cautious consideration at the hands of the government in the near future. These fruits being allowed to come into Canada free are taking the place of fruits which we can produce in Canada and which would be just as suitable for the consumption of the Canadian people. On this question of the free list I wish to give further illustration. We imported into Canada last year $1,376,537 worth of flax seed, and of that large quantity no less than $1,303,758 came from the United States. A fair question to ask would be :	What is the duty on Canadian
flax seed when it seeks admission to the United States ?
The answer is 23 cents a bushel, but when the American farmer seeks a market in Canada for his flax seed it is allowed in free of duty, because this article is on the free list. I have an extract from the 'Citizen,' dated 1903, which reads as follows :

London, March 19.-Mr. Dickson, a prominent linen manufacturer, Leeds, says, after visiting Edmonton district, that nowhere except in Belgium can there he found conditions of soil more favourable to growing flax. He intends to take out his own machinery and erect a mill there this spring.
That shows you, Mr. Speaker, that there are favourable conditions in the Northwest Territories for the production of flaxseed. That is an article of which we Imported last year $1,376,53? worth. I wish to draw the attention of the government to the fact that flaxseed is on the free list and 1 do not think that it is in the interests of our farmers, when we consider that we have so many million acres of land in Canada that are now unoccupied. When we have conditions favourable for the production of this article, I do not think it is fair-play to the farmers and people of Canada that this article should be on the free list, when we import during the twelve months of last year flaxseed to the value I have named. Now, I wish to point out some other products of the farm that require better protection by this government. The duty on butter going to the United States is 6 cents a pound, the Cana dian duty is 4 cents a pound. On cheese the United States duty is 6 cents a pound, and the Canadian duty is 3 cents a pound. I do not wish to be unkind to my hon. friend, but I want to say that I have been particularly careful that my remarks should be directed exclusively to this one question we have up for consideration. When the budget is brought down next week, he will have an opportunity of listening to still larger figures, and I am quite sure if my hon. friend can be convinced he will be convinced that we are (importing altogether too much of every class of goods into this country under this one-sided tariff. Now, I want for a moment to point out how trade is drifting in Canada during the last few years. In 1868 we imported for home consumption from Great Britain, $36,663,695 ; we imported from the United States that same year, $26,315,052. In other words, we imported from Great Britain $10,348,643 more than we did from the United States. But after seven years of our national life had passed away, in 1876, the tables were turned against Great Britain in favour of the United States. In 1876 we imported from Great Britain $40,734,260, and from the United States $46,070,033, showing a balance in favour of the United States in that year of $5,335,773 Ten years more of our national life go by, and in 1886 we imported from Great Britain $40,601,199 and from the United States $44.858,039, showing a balance in favour of the United States of $4,256,840. In 1896 we imported from Great Britain $32,979,742 and from the United States $58,575,024, showing a balance in favour of the United States for that year of $25,594,282. In 1903, the last year of which we have" a complete record, we imported from Great Britain $5S,896,901 and from the "United States $137,605,195, showing a balance in favour of the United States of $78,708,294.

Thus you will see, Mr. Speaker, that our trade is gradually leaving Great Britain and drifting to the United States, and I wish to point out to the right hon. gentleman and his government the fact that one of the reasons, in my humble opinion, is because of the one-sided tariff, the low tariff we have in this country as against the very high tariff that is imposed on our products going into the United States. Some hon. gentlemen will say that our climate is so much against the products of the farm and orchard that we cannot always supply our Canadian market. In no year do the farm products of this country altogether fail in every part of Canada. If we cannot supply the fruit in Ontario, then it can be supplied by the province of Quebec or the maritime provinces. If we cannot supply it in eastern Canada at all, no doubt the time will come when we can produce a very large quantity of it in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, and I am quite sure a considerable portion can be produced in British Columbia. Indeed it is said a very considerable portion of the smaller fruits can be produced in the Yukon district.
I am not going to discuss that now, further than to say that if there is a failure of, for instance, the apple crop in Ontario and there is a good appie crop in other provinces of the Dominion of Canada, then the people in Ontario are sufficiently loyal to bring in their apples from the other provinces of the Dominion rather than to bring them from the United States. The same thing will apply to every other article of produce, pork and every other thing.
The hon. gentleman who to-night occupies the position of Speaker (Mr. Campbell) made some little complaint last year and I wish to refer to what he then said. He dealt at length with the fact that the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) had waited until the budget was brought down before he moved his resolution. My hon. friend made this statement:
I am still in hopes that the tariff will be increased on these articles. I am not going to give up yet ; I am going to continue, and I warn the Finance Minister now that I shall he after him again and again. But so far as I am concerned I am not going to vote for the hon. gentleman's motion.
The hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) spoke in this way, but I shall not pursue that further as the hon. gentleman is now in the chair. I will say, however, that the government have complained in former years during this parliament that we have waited until the budget was brought down before we introduced resolutions of this kind calling for a te-vision of the tariff. I may say to the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his government that we have brought down Mr. BLAIN.
i
the resolution now and that it is a notice not of to-day, but a notice of many years' standing, a notice introduced in this parliament either before or after the budget year after year by the Liberal-Conservative party. That party are prepared vo give our hearty support to the right hon. gentleman and his government in order that a better protection shall be given to the farmers and market-gardeners of this country. When the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues are considering this question-and I presume they are considering it because I was present at a deputation which waited on the hon, the Finance Minister and his colleagues three years ago, and the government held out such hopes to the farmers and market-gardeners that they left Ottawa feeling that, possibly before they got home, the tariff would be revised and everything made right. But three years have passed away and now we are in the fourth session of this parliament. This government came into power in 1890 with a very large majority at their back. A very large majority of the electors of this country supported the right hon. gentleman and his party at the polls so that they had a free hand in tariff as well as other matters and thfcv stood in a unique position, a position such as the Conservative party never found themselves in when revising tariff. The right hon. gentleman is assured of the support of the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and his supporters not only in voice, but in votes recorded in this House on resolutions such as I have read to the House this evening. Therefore, I say that no government has had a better opportunity of correcting this great evil than this government. If ever a government has had fair warning, that warning has been given to the right hon. gentleman and his friends. They have been warned on the floor of this House, newspapers have brought the government's attention to this condition of: things, resolutions by farmers' and market-gardeners' associations have been presented to them, speeches have been made on the subject in this House, resolutions have been voted for, and every possible notice has, been given to this government that they have the support of the Conservative party of this country in attempting to revise the tariff and to make it adequate to meet the wants of the people of Canada, and equal to what is necessary in the interests >
of the farming community of this country who are great contributors to the taxes and who should have a considerable amount of attention from the right hon. gentleman and his government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has gone so fully into this matter that I merely wish to add a few words, because the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and several other constituencies lying - in the vicinity of Montreal, are interested to a very large degree in the question which has been raised by the hon. member for Peel. I shall not go over the figures which have been so carefully grouped by my hon. friend ; they appear in the returns which have been brought down from time to time, but I may say that as he gave them to the House I followed him from these returns, and I found them absolutely correct. The conclusion to which even a superficial examination of these returns inevitably leads is that the importation of garden produce from the United States is increasing gradually from year to year since 1S96, having begun shortly before that time. It has increased steadily and it presses greatly upon important centres in Canada, like Toronto and Montreal, particularly from January to July in every year. From the last returns for which I moved at the beginning of this session that clearly appears. The Americans have an absolute advantage in our markets during the months that might be most profitable to our market-gardeners.
In the months of March, April, May and June, the United States market-gardeners have their harvest. They send their goods in here, and when later in the season our market-gardeners have their products ready for sale, they are prohibited by a high duty from sending them to the United States. Carefully prepared statistics show that of garden products and agricultural products generally, we export to the United States to the equivalent of 10 per cent a head of our population, while we import these products from the United States to the extent of $2.90 cents per head of our population. I was somewhat surprised and at the same
time amused, to hear the Prime Minister state that he could not adopt this amendment because the budget had not yet been brought down ; for I remember that when a similar motion was made by my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) some years ago after the budget speech had been delivered, the tight hon. gentleman's complaint then was that the motion should have been made before the budget speech. I suppose there is no use bothering about the Prime Minister's inconsistency in such a matter. The truth is, that the Prime Minister, his government, and his party have not seriously considered the urgent representations which have been placed before them for the last ten years by the market-gardeners of Canada. The market-gardeners have organized to give their representations strength ; they have sent petitions to the government which were not marked confidential, but which were entitled to no less consideration on that account ; they came to the government in deputation both from Ontario and Quebec, but no heed has been paid to them by the government. I remember, Mr. Speaker, (Mr. Campbell) when you yourself piloted a large deputation of market-gardeners to interview the ministers, and you seemed to be entirely favourable to the claims that were put forward by the gentlemen you accompanied. I am sure it is only the bitter irony of fate that has placed you in the chair to-night, and prevented you from supporting by your voice, and voting as you no doubt would in favour of this amendment. I respectfully point out to the Prime Minister, that the protection which market-gardeners receive on their industry amounts to two per cent only, whereas other industries are protected to a much greater extent. The market-gardeners pay a duty of from twenty-five to thirty-five per cent on everything they consume, but their own industry receives virtually no protection at nil. The industry for which we now plead is not a small industry. We have gone to the trouble of compiling statistics in Jacques Cartier county, and we have found that in that county over a quarter million dollars is invested in the industry, and that there are
2.000	people whose means of livelihood it is. Mr. Legare, leading member of the market-gardeners association, in the province of Quebec, demonstrated to the government when he appeared before it here with a deputation, that if the industry were protected to a reasonable degree it would afford a means of livelihood for not
2.000	but for 6.000 people. On one occasion when a deputation appeared before the government the objection was taken that the consumers should be considered, but it was clearly proved that the consumer does not get these vegetables any cheaper than if he purchased those of native growth. It was shown that on the island of Montreal there could be cultivated at all seasops of

tlie year, tomatoes, beans, celery, lettuce, parsley, onions, cucumbers, cauliflowers, watercress, spinach, green pease, and all those vegetables that come from the United States. It was established that we could not only furnish all the wants of the people of Montreal, but furnish them at a lower price and of better quality. The vegetables sent to us from the United States are what are left over on the markets of Boston and New York, and which are ten or twelve or fifteen days old when they reach here. They are sent in train lohds of twelve or thirteen cars at a time. The importation is increasing from year to year, because while previous to 1897 they were only brought by express, they are now brought in refrigerator cars at less cost, and are consequently sold cheaper. They are valued by the customs at comparatively nothing, pay a very low ad valorem duty and are sold at high prices. The consumer gains no advantage in the matter of price, and he gets vegetables of a quality inferior to the native product. Most of these imported vegetables are grown in the southern states where they are cultivated by coloured and Chinese labour.
Under these circumstances, competition by our own market-gardeners is almost impossible. I said a moment ago that as a general rule the duties scarcely amounted to more than 2 per cent. Take as an example celery, which formerly was very much cultivated around Montreal, and was sold at every period of the winter. The cultivation of celery has now very largely been abandoned, because it conies to us in such large quantities from California. It is sold there at from 10 cents to 15 cents a dozen. It pays a duty of 20 per cent ad valorem, or 2 cents or 3 cents a dozen, and it is sold in Montreal at from 75 cents to $1 a dozen. The same thing applies to very large quantities of cu-umbers, tomatoes, cabbages, green pease and beans, spinach and lettuce. We are in a position in the county of Jacques Cartier to furnish lettuce for the city of Montreal all the winter, and our competitors are the American exporters, who send up large quantities of an inferior article, and who are in a position to sell it at a considerable price on the market of Montreal ; but they flood our market, and are in a position to sacrifice that product, and they do a great deal of injury to our gardeners. Last year, for instance, -when the market in Montreal in the early spring was normal, tomatoes were at a reasonable price, and a great many were being brought into the city of Montreal from the county of Jacques Cartier, when one morning over twelve carloads of tomatoes arrived from the United States and were thrown on the market, disturbing the market and ruining the prospect of our market-gardeners for a just and legitimate profit during more than ten days.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has been asked of the government ? The association in the pro-Mr. MONK.
vince of Ontario has deliberated ; the association in the province of Quebec has held counsel ; and, strange to say, before they even conferred together, they came to exactly the same conclusion, and I submit that that conclusion is a reasonable one. They do not ask for a higher tariff than that w-hich the Americans have against us ; but they have come to the conclusion that in the interest of their industry it is necessary that they should have against the American market-gardeners the same protection which the United States have against us, and that is what they ask from the government. It seems to me that that demand is reasonable and just; it has been properly urged before the government, and this is the occasion for the government to take up the matter. If it is impossible for the Minister of Agriculture himself to investigate it or for the Minister of Customs to look into it. let the government have recourse to its usual method of naming a commission to investigate the truth of the allegations contained in the petitions which have been so often brought to the notice of the government. These people, after waiting for seven years, and after having, on each occasion that they have come here to make their representations to the government, received the assurance that their just complaints would be looked into and if possible remedied, have not made much progress, and it is the duty of the government without further delay to do justice to their claims. It was suggested on one occasion to the Minister of Finance that we might adopt a sliding scale of duties which would not interfere with the legitimate business of our market-gardeners during the first six months of the year, and that suggestion seemed to be acceptable to a certain extent to the Minister of Finance. If the government is not disposed to treat the American producers as they treat our producers in this particular line of business, it might at least make a trial of that sliding scale, which would protect our market-gardeners during the season of the year when they might possibly expect to derive some profit from a legitimate industry which is deserving of every encouragement from the government.
Mr. 0. B. HEYD (South Brant). Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman who introduced this resolution had not connected the farmers with it, I would not have risen to make any observations upon it. So far as the products of the market-gardeners are concerned, if the duty were put upon them, there would be one comfort, that it would fall mainly on the rich. But as the hon. gentleman has included the farmers as being petitioners for increased duties, it would be just as well ito see what the result would be to the farmers of this country if the desires of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) were carried out. The hon. gentleman stated that we imported more butter from the United

States than we export to that country. That is quite immaterial to me. The question is. how much does the importation of butter from the United States injure the fanners of Canada ? When we look at the figures which I have very hurriedly prepared, we find that last year we imported 658.000 pounds of butter, while in 1901 we produced 141,000,000 pounds. Under these circumstances, how much injufy the importation of 058,000 pounds of butter, probably into British Columbia or some of the Northwest Territories, fardistant from our own great producing centres, would do to the farmers of this country, I cannot really see. When you think of 658,000 pounds imported and 141,000,000 pounds made, each man can figure for himself how much a duty on butter would benefit the farmer. Take cheese : last year our imports of cheese were 269.000 pounds, and our exports to England alone were 229.000000 pounds. How much good would an increased duty on cheese do the farmers of Canada ? Take eggs :	we imported las*
year 772,000 dozen, but the product of Canada was 84,000,000 dozen. How' much harm is being done to the farmers of Canada by the importation of those eggs ? When the hon. gentleman alluded to potatoes, I asked him whether yams were included. He said it w7as Irish potatoes he alluded to. Well, last year we imported 407,000 bushels of potatoes, w'hile we produced 55,000,000 bushels in Canada.
We imported 407,000 bushels while we produced 55,000,000. How much injury is the farmer suffering from that import ? Take the question of hay. we imported 7,000 tons last year and produced 8.000.000 tons. Of wheat we imported 84,000 bushels while our production amounted to 93,000.000 bushels. Our imports of oats were 100,000 bushels last year and our product 151,000,000 bushels. Of barley wre imported none, and grew 34,000.000 bushels. Then in the case of apples, while our imports amounted to but 81,000 bushels, the products of our orchards reached the figures of 48,000.000. How could it possibly conduce to the welfare of the farmers to increase the duties upon these articles, w'hieh do not come at all into competition with wbat they raise ? We export more than we import, and the small quantity we do import does not come into competition with the produce of our own farmers. I would not have alluded to this were it not that my hon. friend included the farmers in his resolution. Of pineapples we purchased $127,000 worth. Of bananas-

speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to misinterpret my remarks. I did not say that the resolution asked for a duty on pineapples or bananas, but I distinctly said that these were on the free list but would have to be considered by the government at some future day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
Of course the condition of the artisans of Canada is so prosperous today that they can afford to eat pineapples, bananas, oranges and other luxuries of that kind. They eat pineapples to the extent of $127,000 worth, bananas to the extent of $819,000 worth, and oranges and lemons to the extent of $1,000,000 worth. What the object of the hon. gentleman was in introducing these articles into his speech at all I cannot conceive, unless it were to show that our people are consuming too many luxuries in this period of good times, and that* we must by some means put a stop to that consumption and compel them to eat more dried apples. It was said once by some English statesman that the people of England would be more prosperous if they ate less. On the same principle, our friend thinks that our people would be more prosperous if they were prevented from eating pineapples', bananas and orangess. But my hon. friend from Essex (Mr. Cowan) says these fruits are not grown up there, and what they cannot grow in Essex you cannot grow anywhere else in Canada. The tax upon oranges, pineapples and bananas, therefore, would be a tax on the consumer and for whose benefit ? It could not be for the benefit of the farmers or market-gardeners, for they do not grow these fruits.
I am quite willing to admit that a few men in Canada who engage in the market-gardening business would benefit by having their interests protected to a certain extent, but it is a large question whether the great body of consumers should be subjected to a tax of that kind for the benefit of a few. Personally I have no objection when the tpx falls" on the rich, but bananas and oranges are sold so low that even the poorest of our people can buy them. The banana is a wholesome food, bought principally by the poorer classes, as I can state from my personal knowledge, being in the business of selling these articles myself.
I do not think that my hon. friend has strengthened his case by including these articles in his list or by trying to show that our farmers are injured by an importation of farm products, when the relative quantity of that import, compared with our own production, is represented by one to a thousand. Just imagine the harm that is done our farmers by 531.000 pounds of imported butter coming into competition with 141,000,000 pounds,; which they produce, and by the importation of $50,000 worth of cheese. And what kind of cheese ? Stilton, Roquefort, Swiss, and I suppose even Lim-burger. And these cheeses, which are regarded as luxuries and found upon the tables of the principal hotels and of the rich, are supposed to come into competition with our cheese industry, which exports to Great Britain 229,000,000 pounds, besides giving an abundant supply to 6,000,000 of our own people. The whole thing is absurd, and I trust the House will vote down this resolution.

speechtext: I was rather surprised, Mr. Speaker, to hear the speech we have just had from the hon. gentleman who has just taken Ms seat, and who last year wanted more protection on a manufacturing industry situated in the city from which he comes. But while he is quite prepared to stand up for protection for a particular industry in which he is interested, he is quite ready to vote down a motion which, asks for protection to the produce of our farms. The argument he lias advanced furnishes proof positive that our farmers require protection, because to the extent that farm products are brought in from the United States, to that extent must our farmers seek a far-off market for what stuff they grow.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Tell us how you can protect cheese.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
We can protect it to the extent that cheese comes in from the United States to this country. You may import Limburger cheese or anything else, our Canadian cheese is quite good enough for our Canadian people. The hon. gentleman went on to show how many potatoes were imported and how many we could not use, but just to the amount of foreign potatoes brought into this country must be consumed here, does this foreign product drive our own to a distant foreign market ? That operates in the same way as bringing in free corn displaces so much of the coarse grains as would be consumed on our farms. These hon. gentlemen talk about our not producing sufficient market-garden stuff iq the Dominion, but they do not give fair play to our market-gardeners to produce anything like what they would if they had sufficient tariff protection. They could produce many months earlier than they do now. because they could afford to build hot houses to a greater extent. At present it is not worth a market-gardener's while to go into a big speculation by building hot houses and glass houses in order to supply this country with early vegetables when the Americans are charged so small a tariff on the products they send in. If the tariff were high enough to shut out the imported stuff, our market-gardeners could grow a great deal more and during many more months. When the sugar beet growers of Ontano waited on this government and asked for a protection or a bounty on the glowing of sugar beets they could not get a bounty, but the government proposed instead to give a bounty to the manufacturers of the beet root sugar and let them fix the price to the farmers. I cannot see why the farmers should not be protected as well as the manufacturers. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Heyd) was anxious that the binder twine business should be given a bounty, but I do not think that he would have urged such a policy if there were not a binder twine factory in his town. I am Mr. HEYD.
in favour of giving the farmer the same fair-play that you ask for the manufacturers. I remember the late Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) giving a protectionist speech at South Ontario, and I wrell remember the Reformers clapping their hands "'hen he spoke of protection for the farmers and manufacturers of Oshawa. And he almost goes over the same speech he made in Oshawa, and the very ones who applauded him there hiss him in this House. If it was a good thing to give bounties on steel, on lead, on lumber and other things, why do you refuse to give a bounty on sugar beets, when these are grown by our own farmers ? Every hundredweight of vegetables brought into Canada displaces Canadian-grown stuff, and injures the Canadian farmer by compelling him to seek a foreign market and to accept the lower price that is offered when it reaches that market, instead of the price that should be got for the product fresh and perfect for use in the home market. There is no argument in favour of a bounty to a factory in the town of the last speaker (Mr. Heyd) that would not be equally strong in favour of bounties to the farmers, who are the back bone of this country. If we use American farm products, that means that a certain quantity of our own products must be sent to the old country for sale. And in this the American gains the benefit, because our market, in which the American sells his stuff, is comparatively near, while the market in which our people must sell is distant. I hope, not from a party standpoint, that the farmers and market-gardeners of this country will be given as good protection as the manufacturers. But you cannot give protection, even to the manufacturers, without benefiting the farmers,, because the farmers will get the benefit from the sale of their goods in the nearer market created by the presence of the workers in the fac tories.

speechtext:
This question of protection to the farmers and market-gardeners did not come up from the time when I first had the honour of a seat in this House, in 1896, until the session of 1902. The question was then raised by my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard). That hon. gentleman had been elected in 1902, and I must say that this question of higher duties in favour of the farmers was one of the issues in the cam paign which was carried on in his county. He brought up the question in this House, and was seconded in his efforts by the hon! member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), who was then leader of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec. I well remember the speeches of both these gentlemen during the session of 1902. It ap pears that the hon. member from Jacques Cartier was found deficient in some way by the hon. gentlemen opposite. True, he was

the only one who had carried an election, wlio had gained a victory, in the province or Quebec since the general elections of 1896. But it appears that this year, in the month of March, he was forced out of the leadership by the members of his party, who selected as their leader, the gentleman who is supposed to be the high priest of protection in this country. That gentleman, the hon. member for St. Mary's, (Mr. Tarte), had occasion to speak during the session of 1902, and it will be well, perhaps, to remind the House of the speech he delivered on that occasion, Mark well, Mr. Speaker, he was chosen as the leader of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec because he was the apostle of high protection in this country. And what did he say on this very question in the session of 1902, answering my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier and my hon. friend from Laval, who had used at that time the same arguments which we have heard in support of the resolution now before the House ' The hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) was then Minister of Public Works. Speaking on April 28th, 1902, he said :
My hon. friend wants us to raise the duties upon lettuce, cucumbers, tomatoes, asparagus, I celery, beets, onions, &c. It is well known that in the winter months we do not grow cabbages nor cucumbers. We are also aware that it is extremely difficult to raise tomatoes in the winter season. We had to pay, last winter, 50 cents a pound for tomatoes of Canadian growth, whilst American tomatoes were being sold on the Montreal market at 20 cents a pound.
Remember, this is the apostle of high protection who speaks. Further on he says :
It is idle to appeal to prejudices. There are enough people buying tomatoes and lettuce, for let it be known that I am speaking the plain unvarnished truth. Cauliflowers are not grown in the winter months in Canada. I agree that during a certain season of the year they can be kept, perhaps during two or three months. The cauliflowers we buy in the winter are imported from the United States.
In short I believe that what the hon. gentleman is aiming at is to make political capital with the electors and to catch popular favour rather than appealing to their reason. Let my hon. friend allow me in all due deference, to call his attention to the fact that in the province of Quebec, as elsewhere, farmers have a great deal of common sense. Go through the county of Laval and ask the market-gardeners if thpy can produce cucumbers, celery, tomatoes and cauliflowers in the winter months, and they will tell you that they cannot do so.
Further on, answering the hon. member for Laval, the Minister of Public Works of that day used the following language :
My hon. friend knows very well that, even if additional duties were imposed on pease, tomatoes. cucumbers and other vegetables, that would neither improve the climate nor enable us to grow those vegetables to advantage during the winter months. The increase in the duties asked for by my hon. friend would only
result in forcing the consumer to pay more for those products, w'ithout improving the condition of the Canadian producer. To my mind, such a proposition is preposterous.
This is the language of the high priest of protection in this Dominion. I might say that, even after my hon. and distinguished friend from Jacques Cartier had fought the battle in the county of Laval, where this question of high protection for market gardeners had been made a live issue, he was deposed as leader and replaced by the hon. gentleman from St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte). And here we have Mr. T-arte's own words against the very proposition which is now under discussion on the motion of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain). For my part, I hold that the hon. member for St. Mary's spoke on that occasion, words of wisdom. And I am ready to stand by him during this debate, and to say with him that the farmers and market-gardeners of the Montreal district- and of the GaspS district, too-have a great deal of common sense, and will not be caught by the silly proposition which has been made this evening.

(Translation.) I have listened with pleasure to the views expressed by the hon. Solicitor General concerning the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). Two years ago the ex-minister was opposing the doctrine laid down in the amendment which the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has just presented, but since he has grown older and come to the conclusion, or rather he is convinced, that we should concede the fair demands of the people of Laval and several counties submitted to you through the channel of the member now addressing the House. Every one remembers, Mr. Speaker, that he who is just now addressing you was returned in spite of the combined efforts of both the provincial and Dominion governments, at the request and upon the advice of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). Notwithstanding anything which the hon Solicitor General may have said, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier was not deprived of his leadership by the Conservatives in the province of Quebec. If the hon. Solicitor General is not any more familiar with the effect of the present tariff upon market gardening in Canada than he is with the internal administration of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec. I am bound to admit that he does not know much about it.
It is useless for my hon. friend, the Solicitor General, to wax eloquent in order to stir up the Conservatives of the province of Quebec who are of one mind in honouring the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. The Conservatives can dispense with the advice of my hon. friend when selecting the chieftain who is to lead them to victory at the next general election. He is strangely mistaken if he imagines that he can stir up in

our midst strifes altogether unknown in tlie Conservative party.
As to these customs duties, I do not intend to answer the so-called arguments which have just now been brought forward, but speaking as a representative from the district of Montreal, I shall avail myself of this opportunity to state openly that my hon. friend, the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was not turned down by the Conservatives of Quebec but that he willingly resigned, actuated by purely personal motives.
My hon. friend the Solicitor General attempted to make merry of the ex-Minister of Public Works because be opposed this amendment in 1902.
I did not rise on my feet to recall what I said two years ago when answering the remarks of the ex-Minister of Public Works. When the hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte) rose at that time to oppose the resolution which I had had the honour to introduce in the House, he was not as familiar as he is to-day with the needs of the farmers in the neighbourhood of large cities, and I may say that he has since so stated to me. Having considered the question, he has come to the conclusion propounded by the hon. member for Peel and the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, viz., that the market gardeners need a larger measure of protection.
I see in ' Hansard,' Mr. Speaker, -(Mr. Campbell), that even yourself you favoured increasing the customs duties on garden truck brought in from abroad, and I am convinced that, were it not for political considerations, and the fear of offending your leader and master, you would give a free vote in favour of the resolution now under consideration.
It is not my intention to repent now what I had occasion to say on this question during the sessions of 1902 and 1903. However, as I have seconded the motion of the hon. member for Peel, all I can say is that the same needs exist to-day. We were told during former sessions when we brought up this question that it was too late. This year it was our desire to remove that ob'ection by springing this question in the early days of the session. Yourself. Mr. Speaker (Mr. Campbell), you took part in the discussion in 1902 and 1903. In 1903, yon told us that it was too early and. in 1903. that it was too late to introduce that resolution.
This year we put the question before the House previous to the budget being brought down. The right hon. leader of the House told us a while ago that we should have waited until the budget speech had been delivered. I considered the suggestion as another attempt to evade the question without settling it one way or the other. I hope that the hon. member for Teel .(Mr. Plain) will press this motion to the end. so that if the government should decide to move in the matter, they may rely on the vote that will be g'ven to-night.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
Without going into details, I may say that what the gardeners are asking for, is a specific duty, because the present tariff with its ad valorem duty opens the door to too many fraudulent devices on the part of the importers of foreign fruits.
I would not feel disposed to make any charges against the custom officers, but it is a w'ell known fact, at least among the buyers in Montreal, that these officers whose duty it is to examine all the vegetables coming from abroad, admit all those from the United States as damaged goods, even if they are in prime condition ; in that way the American exporters can flood the Canadian market to the detriment of the home producers who are not in a position to compete successfully.
Before concluding, I must say that gardeners from the counties around Montreal, as well as those from the counties surrounding our large cities, as Toronto and others, would be satisfied if the government decided to put on all the articles enumerated in this resolution, the same duty as is exacted by our American neighbours on the same articles.
I hope. Mr. Speaker, after the speech of the right hon. first minister, that we will succeed in our exertions to obtain a revision of the tariff to the advantage of the gardeners of this country. I flatter myself that my efforts in that direction have not been in vain, and that my election as a member of this Hbuse will not have been without some weight, when the government comes to the decision of increasing the duty on the market garden products.

'

Liberal candidates were in the field, and the outcome was a split among our friends, and then there was the natural flow of sympathy for a man of the county as against an outsider.
It seems to me that the hon. gentlemen opposite have failed to make out their case. They have not proved that the American products are slaughtered on our markets ; they have not established that the gardening industry is not prosperous in this country. It is my good fortune, Mr. Speaker, to be professionally in touch with the gardeners of the surrounding counties of Montreal and I know personally that there is not a more prosperious class in this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
I am sure the House is deeply indebted to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) for again introducing a subject which is as much a live question to-day as it was on the former occasion when it was brought to the attention of the House. In my opinion the home market of Canada, to the agriculturist, the market-gardener, the producer of fruits and vegetables, as well as all the other commodities produced on the farm, is the very best asset he has. It is of more value to him than all the other markets of the world, because it consumes from 80 to 90 per cent of the entire products of the farm. I say therefore it is of the utmost importance that the home market should be guarded by every legitimate means this government can employ for preserving to the people of this country such a valuable asset. If a foreign nation were to invade our shores I have no doubt the Minister of Militia and Defence, whom I am glad to see in his place, would at once call upon all the forces at his command to drive back the enemy and to prevent the invasion. Now I believe it is just as legitimate, just as proper that the Finance Minister of this country should use the tariff of which he has the making for the purpose of preventing an invasion of our country by the surplus products of the United States and other countries. I say the one is just as legitimate as the other, and no one for a moment, not even yourself, Mr. Speaker, would object to the Minister of Militia using all the means in his power to prevent a territorial invasion of our country by a foreign enemy. Surely the invasion of our market by the surplus products of foreign countries is just as injurious; and therefore you. Sir, should join us, and I trust you will join us on this occasion, in supporting the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Peel, and give better protection to the home market of Canada for the products of our farms.
For 25 years this policy has been the declared policy of Canada. In 1878 the national policy was brought down, and then it was declared to be the policy of this country to protect the agricultural products of Canada. It is ti-ue that a portion of that
protection has been removed. I regret very much that in the tariff of 1897 the hon. gentlemen now in power so far forgot their duty to the agriculturists of this country as to reduce the duties on important products of the farm ; and I regret as well that coming in under changed conditions, changed circumstances, when larger protection to the agricultural products of the country was necessary, they did not see fit to grant to that class that fair share of national care to which their position, their wealth and their numbers fairly entitle them.	,	,
My intention to-night, Mr. Speaker, is to advert more particularly to the growth of small fruits ; the matter of vegetables has been referred to by others. Permit me first to make a brief reference to some remarks that fell from the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd). He seemed to try to laugh away the idea of protecting the farmer on his butter, his cheese and his pork, simply because the importations of butter, cheese and pork were comparatively small compared with the entire production of the country. Now, I want for a moment or two to show that hon. gentleman that this is not a matter that can be laughed away. The farmers of this country are deeply interested in this question, and if the importations of pork from the United States are not large compared with the entire products of Canada in that article, it is no argument why protection should be removed or should not be increased. Take the item of barrel pork alone. Last year, I find we imported 5,637,000 pounds of barrel pork, a very considerable item indeed. But what I want to draw attention to is this fact. We are told that the great market for our bacon and ham is in England, we send the greater part of that portion of our pork to the British market, and we are told that it is no difference whether our market is protected or not because we have a market in England for all the bacon and ham we can produce. But, Mr. Speaker, neither the hon. member for Brant, nor any other gentleman in this House, has been able to find a hog that will cut up entirely into bacon and hams. There are portions of the hog. as the hon. gentleman will understand, of which you cannot make bacon and hams, a portion of the hog for which you cannot find a profitable market in Great Britain. While you can export your bacon and hams, all that we can produce for that matter, you- cannot export certain other portions of the hog. You cannot, for example, find in England a market for all our lard ; our pork packers cannot find a market in England for the shoulders, for the spare ribs and for other portions of the hog, backs and so forth-yes, and the heads and feet. These portions of the hog cannot be profitably exported to Great Britain and must be sold in Canada. Now, Sir, if we allow our market to be invaded by

American pork to such an extent that it will prevent our pork packers from finding a market for the unexportable part of the hog, what are our pork packers to do ? They have simply to do one of two things. Notwithstanding that they have a market in Britain for all their bacon and ham, if they cannot find a market in Canada for the unexportable part of the hog they simply have to reduce the price of live hogs to the farmer or stop their business. Now in 1902 there were more hogs slaughtered in the province of Ontario than in any previous year. What was the result? There was so much of the unexportable part of the hog thrown upon the market in addition to what came in from the United States, that the home market could not consume them, and we had not a profitable market abroad for such. The result was that the pork packers of this country had to reduce the price to the farmers very materially indeed. That will be the result. We can find a market, as I said before, for our bacon and ham, all we can produce, but we must guard the market of Canada as regards that portion of the animal, which we cannot export to the old country. Therefore, I say that to laugh at the idea of a duty on pork being necessary because only a small amount is being imported, is not treating the question with that sincerity to which it is entitled.
Now, Sir, with reference to the small fruit production I desire to say a few words.
1 think, Mr. Speaker, (Mr. Campbell) you are authority for the statement made a year ago that some 4,000 people in the neighbourhood of the city of Toronto were employed in the production of garden stuff. We have it stated here to-night by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that some 2,000 people are employed in his own county. Now I would not undertake to say how many people are employed in the county I have the honour to represent, in the production of small fruit, but I know it is a very large number indeed, men, women and children, who are engaged in growing, gathering and marketing small fruit. It is an industry of considerable importance, an industry in which a very considerable amount of capital is invested. The land on which these small fruits are grown is very valuable, is worth hundreds and hundreds of dollars per acre. No land suitable for that purpose can he bought at a cheap price.
As I said before, a very considerable number of people are employed and these people are entitled to consideration at the hands of the government in having a market provided for their product at their door. Small fruits such as raspberries and strawberries cannot be exported to Great Britain ; practically they cannot be exported to the United States, because the people of the United States produce the same fruits in large quantities and have a tariff against our fruits which guards their market. I say therefore that we are Mr. HENDERSON.
entitled to the paternal care of the government so that we can retain the market that we have in our own country for these perishable products. I am aware that when I advance an idea of this kind I shall be met with the stock argument- and I think it has been thrown across the floor to-night-that if you put an increased duty on these green fruits you will enhance the price to the consumer. Suppose it does enhance the price to the consumer, who is going to be benefited by it ? The farmer, the man we want to help. Is it any harm to help the farmer to make more profits out of his farm so long as you do not hurt any one else ? But with a proper readjustment of the tariff there is no reason why the consumer should be hurt because we can protect the consumer at the same time that we protect the producer. We can protect the producer by increasing the duty on small fruits coming into this country and keeping out foreign fruit, so as to give the gardener and the farmer of Canada who produce the small fruits a larger and better market for their products. On the other hand you can, by a readjustment of the tariff, protect the man who consumes fruit in another way. Reference was made to the importation of dried fruits. We import very largely into this country, currants, raisins and prunes. The prunes come chiefly from California, raisins come from Spain as well as from California, and currants largely from Greece. We do not produce any of these articles in this country. We might put a duty of five hundred per cent on these articles, but you could not protect the industry in this country. A duty put on these dried fruits is not for the purpose of protection, but for revenue purposes, and revenue purposes only. Now let us simply readjust the tariff on fruits ; let us reduce the duty on the dried fruits and increase it on the green, and what is the result ? The result would be that the farmer in Canada who produces the strawberries, raspberries, currants and grapes would get a larger market and a better price for his products and when any family wants to buy groceries, their raisins, currants, prunes, and other dry fruits of which they would buy more pounds per year than of green fruits, they would get them at a much reduced price, because the duty would be lower. Thus there is no reason with the readjustment of the tariff, why any one would be hurt. But there is a strong probability that a very deserving class in this community would be helped. Therefore, I say, if the Minister of Finance wants to help the farmers of this country he has an opportunity of doing so without hurting the consumers or causing any families to pay a larger price for the fruits they consume during the whole year. The answer of the Finance Minister is : Our policy is a policy of tariff for revenue only,
(

we cannot afford to do that. The Finance Minister will tell us that if he reduces the duty on the dried fruits he will lose the revenue from them and that if he increases the duty on the green fruit, fewer of them would come in and he. would get less revenue. Tlie\ Minister of Finance wants revenue ; he cares nothing for the interest of the people of this country, he cares not whether the farmers get a proper price for their products or not. No, Sir, that is not the first consideration of the tariff of this government. Their tariff as they have told us is a tariff for revenue only, and it is framed in such a way as will take the greatest amount of taxes out of the people irrespective of what the people's interests are. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) would use the same argument with other articles it would simply show how unfair the argument is. Apply the argument to raw sugar, or to nice or an article like foreign leaf tobacco, as well as the articles 1 have given, imported raisins and currants and prunes. In every case a tax on these articles goes to enhance the price. If you put an extra duty on raw sugar you certainly enhance the price. A duty is not placed on raw sugar for purposes of protection ; we make refined sugar, but do not make raw sugar and the higher you put the duty on raw sugar the higher the price to the consumer becomes. The Minister of Finance says that is all right. Tariff for revenue is his policy ; he cares not for the interests of the people of this country, he cares not whether the farmer makes a profit so long as he gets $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 to expend in this country.	The
same thing applies to rice on which he imposes a duty of about sixty-one per cent. You cannot produce rice in this country and a duty placed on rice is simply a tax on the people, and the same thing applies to the other articles I have mentioned.
Readjusting the tariff on the fruits that I have suggested would be a benefit to the farmer, the gardener, the workman and the business man. A larger market would be secured and there would be more employment for labour and, as I said before, if it does enhance the price of goods, no one is hurt because the tariff can be readjusted, so that by levelling it, in reducing the duty on dried fruit and increasing it on green fruit any family can secure the requisite supply of fruits during the whole year at no greater cost, while the producer of fruits in this country will be largely benefited. I do not desire at this late hour to detain the House, but I would like to refer to the large importation of dried and green fruits into this country.
I do not desire to give the matter in detail. but let me say that we imported in 1903 for home consumption in blackberries, raspberries, gooseberries aiyl strawberries alone 1,066,035 pounds, enough to keep a good many gardeners employed.
We imported of cuerries, 146,956 pounds. We imported of grapes, 1,151,249, and let me tell you that about one half of these grapes came from the United States.
We imported of canned goods in 1903. 1,608,749 pounds valued at $83,545. Of this amount of canned goods 730,064 pounds came from the United States and under the jjre-ferential tariff we received 718,368 pounds. Every pound of these goods could be grown in Canada, and put up in Canadian factories. The United States sent us last year $41,564 worth of canned fruit, and they took from us $13,891 worth, a very unfair exchange indeed, and an exchange which proves that we should have a bigger share of their market if we are going to let them have so large a share of ours. We imported last year 27,372,811 pounds of dried fruits ; so that you see that it is quite possible by slightly reducing the duty on the dried fruits to furnish revenue to the government, and to make compensation to the householders of this country for any enhanced cost they may be put to by reason of the increased duty on the green fruit. I am sure that the House will welcome this amendment. It gives us an opportunity of showing to the Finance Minister on the eve of his budget speech, just what the people of this country desire. I know, Mr. Speaker, (Mr. Campbell) your strong opinions on this question. I know you realize just as well as we do that the market-gardeners and producers of small fruits around the city of Toronto and throughout Canada are suffering by reason of the invasion of foreigners on their limited market. We hope that the First Minister will inform the Finance Minister of the views we have expressed, and that when he brings down the budget on Tuesday next there will be an adjustment of the duties on vegetables and small fruits, such as will inure to the best interests of the producers as well as the- consumers in this country.

The Prime Minister devoted less than a minute by the watch, to the discussion of this important question ; he waived it aside with indifference, and he told us we would know the mind of the government when we heard the budget speech. Is-it not well that the government should know the sense of the House on this question, before that budget speech is delivered ? The only other member of the government who spoke was the Solicitor General, and he simply told us what the Hon. Mr. Tarte had said on a former occasion, and then he sat down sn tisfied. I sympathize with you to-night Mr. Speaker (Mr. Campbell'). I know this has been a painful scene to you. You headed a deputation that waited on the Minister of Finance with regard to this important question, and not many months ago you delivered an eloquent and earnest speech that came from your heart and not from your lips, in favour of the principle of the amend-

ment which is now before the House. I sympathize with you that you are compelled to-night to occupy the painful position of listening in silence to the jibes and. jeers ol the member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) against the market-gardeners and the farmers of this country. His remarks must have pained you. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) would compel the market-gardeners of this country to eat dried apples and Limburger cheese for having the temerity of petitioning this House for redress of their grievances. The hon. member for Brant spoke for the government. He is very prominent in_the county of Brant, but let me remind the House that he is a large importer of these very articles from the United States, on which we think a duty should be placed. It is this gentleman that the government gets to speak for them, and it is this gentleman who ridicules the farmers of this country.

Mr. CLANCY,
Mr. CiLANCY. Will the hon. gentleman say that these reductions were not made ?

Mr. CLANCi'. Was the hon. gentleman opposed to them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: What an independent position the hon. gentleman takes ; what little t responsibility he takes. No charge could be laid at his door. He knows nothing about it ; he is not responsible, and he is scarcely < ognizant that it ever took place. What was that done for ? It was done for the purpose of bolstering up and encouraging an industry in the hon. gentleman's own town which was perishing, and the government of the day had not the courage to impose protective duties, but, to compensate, they made a reduction in the duties on the taw material ; and what happened ? Perhaps the hon. gentleman does not know that the doors of that establishment in hi, own town have been closed for the want of reasonable protection. But the hon. gentleman was not satisfied with that. He supported and voted for the taking of the duty off binder twine ; and what is he doing now? Supporting a government which taxes the farmers and market-gardeners, and makes them pay tribute to the manufacturers of binder twine by way of bounties, because the duties have been taken away. The hon. gentleman is almost every day making the life of the Finance Minister unhappy by going to him and urging him to put a duty of $5 apiece on carriages to assist an industry in his own town. Perhaps he will deny that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
As this is the first time I am free to vote for this resolution, I wish to say a few words. I was unable to vote for it on the two former occasions, except in so far as a pair may be considered a vote, because each time I happened to be paired with a government member. I wish to say that I fully concur in the remarks of my hon. friend fromj Peel (Mr. Blain) and of those who support him from this side. I regret that I could not understand the language in which my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) spoke, but I venture to guess that probably his constituents will have as difficult a task to understand the arguments he made and the stand he has taken. With respect to the hon. gentleman from Gaspe iMr. Lemieux),' who quoted the argument made use of by the hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte), who was then a cabinet minister, and who argued that the Canadian market-gardeners could not grow market-garden stuff during the winter months and therefore it was not advisable to increase the duty, and I am informed that the market-gardeners waited on the government and asked for an increase in the tariff. When the argument was used that they could not produce vegetables during the winter months, they said they were willing to accept a sliding scale. That is to say that during the winter months, when it was held they could not produce the vegetables they should be charged duty on a sliding scale and that would not prevent the Americans coming in. But in the season when they could produce vegetables they asked that a sliding scale should be so adjusted as to prevent American competition. That is the difference between the argument then and now.
Now, with respect to the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) we all know that it was his constitutional duty to take the position he did at that time. Knowing that a majority of the cabinet were opposed to an increase of duty, what other course had he as a cabinet minister? Could we expect him to rise in his place and condemn the policy that the government themselves had decided upon ? Certainly not. But, as soon as he left the cabinet and he left it because the majority of his colleagues were opposed to reasonable protection for the industries of this country-he published an article in the newspaper with which he

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: is connected repudiating the arguments used in support of the position he had taken on the protection of market-gardeners. \t hen he was free to express his opinions the opinions he expressed were the direct opposite from those we have heard from the hon. member, for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux). Some attention lias been paid to the remarks of my hon. friend from South' Brant (Mr. Heyd). I was sorry to hear that hon. gentleman speak as he did. He is eager to protect the manufacturers in the city of Brantford because they are his constituents. In a sneering way he alluded to the fact that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Biain) had mentioned farmers, and the hon. member (Mr. Ilyed) thought he should have confined himself to the market-gardeners. He mentioned several articles on which the farmers of this county had protection. But he opposed the increase of the duty on butter, cheese and eggs and other articles produced by our farmers. Is it not true that the agriculturists of the United States produce more than the people of the 'United States consume, and yet they find it necessary to have a duty of six cents a dozen on eggs, double the duty on butter that we have, and double the duty on cheese ? The Canadian agriculturists also produce more than we consume. In all fairness we should put the Canadian farmer on at least as good a plane as the Americans. What objections then, can the government have to putting on-duty for duty with the United States ? My hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) quoted oats. And here is a most remarkable thing that is shown by the tables of imports and exports. No farmer in this country, nobody who knows the faets, will deny that the agriculturists in this country can raise as good oats as those of the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Better.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
I am not a farmer, and' so am not in a position to speak of this matter from my own knowledge. But I am glad to be informed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Morin) that we can, produce better oats than the United States. But I would like to point out that, while the Canadian farmers accepted 30 cents a bushel for their oats sent to the United States, Americans received fifty cents a bushel for oats brought into this country. I find that we exported to the United States 120,702 bushels of oats, for which we received $39,062. We imported into Canada 100,811 bushels of oats, for which the purchasers paid $50,896. That is to say, the Americans received $11,844 more for about 100,000 bushels of oats than we received for about 120,000 bushels. Now,
I say that if we had our own markets for the Canadian farmer, instead of being obliged to pay a duty of 15 cents a bushel on oats, going into the American market, while the American farmer can send oats into this country under a duty of 10 cents, which should be 15 cents a bushel, we would have

a better market at home. It is celarly the duty of the government to increase our duty to 15 cents a bushel as 1 said before. Now, in looking over twenty-one different articles of the farmer and market-gardener, I find that the Americans sent into Canada $3,664,201 in excess of what we sent to them. 1 may say to hon. gentlemen opposite that I do not include the item of 6.033,898 bushels of free corn valued at $3,250,329, nor am I including wheat, the import of which amounted to $556,705. Of course, it may be said that this was not consumed in this country. I am willing to admit that, and so I am not including it in this calculation.
1 notice hon. gentlemen opposite who represent constituencies in the Northwest smile at all this and treat it as a joke. Yet I find that in 1903 we exported to the United States only 1,907 horses, valued at $340,239, while we imported from the United States 29,59S horses, valued at $790,169. And the government supporters from the Northwest a ifew years ago were complaining bitterly because the Minister of Finance and this government did not increase the minimum valuation of horses to be imported into this country-in other words did not increase the duty. Then take cattle, another important item with our friends from the Northwest. We exported to the United States 10,432 head, valued at $292,288, while we imported into this country 37.527 head, valued at $472,689. Yet my hon. friend from Brant thinks this is all a joke. He thinks the farmers should not have protection. I am glad that i am to have an opportunity , to record my vote in favour of the Canadian farmers and market-gardeners. And. so long as I occupy a seat in this House I shall take the stand that the farmers of this country are entitled to greater protection than they have to-day. And I hope the party I have the pleasure of belonging to and supporting will make the case so plain that, after the next general election the leader who has the judgment to adopt this policy, will be given the opportunity of carrying that policy into effect. I wish to draw the attention of the Canadian farmer to the fact that this hon. gentleman is a minister of the Crown who rises and opposes this motion. He properly voiced the sentiments of the government, and it must be recognized as the sentiment of the government. And the Canadian farmer wants to know that, and knowing it he will see clearly that he is not likely to receive any protection from this government.
