SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Lots of them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
If he will come to the province of Ontario he will find that marketgardening is a great industry employing thousands. The market-gardeners in the hon. gentleman's (Mr Lemieux's) constituency produce fish, largely. We are willing to afford them protection in their industry and they should be fair enough to protect other industries in this country. ' But the hon. member for Gasp6 is a member of a government that is opposed to this motion. Another man who takes the same position is the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd). He treated the House to an old argument of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), an argument used by that hon. gentleman nearly a quarter of a century ago. an argument which has been for about that length of time exploded, discredited. He quotes the exportation of various lines of products from this country and says : Can you protect the cheese in this country when we export 229,000.000 pounds and only import a few thousand pounds ? Well, what brought about that condition ?
When American cheese was coming in until that industry was being destroyed in this country, it was the duty that was put on cheese and the restrictions surrounding the imports, that enabled the Canadian farmers to secure their own market and then they went into that line to such an extent that last year they exported 229,000,000 pounds of cheese. Would they have been able to export that quantity but for the protection given in 1878 ? No, because filled cheese was coming across the line into Canada and was being exported and branded as Canadian cheese, and the effect was to destroy the reputation of our cheese in the mother country. Canadians were being handicapped because their cheese was losing its reputation. But when a law was passed to prevent that, then the Canadians got the full advantage of the excellent character of their cheese. When a law was passed that gave protection to the Canadian producer of cheese, he developed his industry to such an extent that to-day Canadian cheese has a reputation inferior to none.
The hon. memuer spoke about pork, and asked : Can you protect the farmer in pork ? Does the hon. member for Brant



remember that in 1890 we were importing into Canada no less than 23,000,000 pounds of pork and fresh meats to feed the Canadian people ? Does he remember when the farmers came down here in large deputations and applied to the government to put on a duty ? The government did put on a duty, not as high as the Canadian farmer wished, and the result was that in one year we shut out 13,000,000 pounds of that pork. What is pork selling for today ? Remember that the imports did not include the head and feet, and portions of the hog which were of little value, because it did not pay to import them. 13,000,000 pounds of pork at 10 cents a pound would represent $1,300,000, so much of an additional market for the Canadian farmers. AVas that no benefit, no protection to him ? It is useless to tell the Canadian farmer that he had no additional market on account of the national policy in 1890, because he will tell you that you do not know what you are talking about. When the farmers began to get a profitable return for their pork after one year of this policy, that industry began to develop until it has reached its present great proportions. That duty did keep out American pork and is keeping it out to-day. It is true it is still coming in to some extent, and some of the duties need to be readjusted because of changed conditions ; pork is coming in in larger quantities than it should.
AVliat I have said with regard to pork applies equally to butter, to cheese and to other articles in that line. The hon. member says we cannot protect the Canadian farmers in 'butter. Does he remember when we passed a law to shut out oleomargarine, butterine and those substitutes for Canadian butter that were injuring the market for our butter ? His own friends a few years ago tried to take credit for passing that law, as they endeavoured to take credit for it one or two years ago.. And yet the hon. member for Brant asks, can you protect Canadian butter ? He need not ask that question of the Canadian farmer. He says, can you protect Canadian oats when we only imported 100,000 bushels last year and raised over 100,000,000 bushels ? AVhy did we import that small quantity ? Because we put on a duty that shut out American oats that was coming in by the million bushels, and the Canadian farmer to-day has his own market by virtue of that law. And yet we are told that you cannot protect the Canadian farmer. Sir, it is well that the Canadian farmer should know who are his friends in this House and who are his opponents. I say if this discussion served no other purpose than to show the Canadian farmer which party is opposed to his interest and which party is supporting it, it would still be well worth the time we are giving it. The hon. member voiced the sentiment of his party no doubt, and of his friends on that side of the Mr. SPROULE.
House. But why should the 'Canadian farmer expect anything from the present government ? Did they not tell the Canadian farmer that they were not in favour of protection, but in favour of a revenue duty only ? They have now a duty which gives them ample revenue, more than enough, why should they give the Canadian farmer any more protection ? Why give the Canadian manufacturer any more protection ? The tariff, they declared, is a better one than the tariff in force when they came into power, and gives them ample revenue, therefore the Canadian farmer need not look for any more protection, either for his garden stuff or for his produce in any other line. The then hon. member for South Oxford (Sir Richard Cartwright >
said : We are not supposed to protect the farmers. AA7hen they appealed to the government of that day to put on a duty, what was his reply ? All he could tell them to do was to work harder and eat less. That is the only consolation he gave the poor farmer who was beat out of the markets of his own country. The sooner the farmers know who are their friends in this House and this country the better for them. ' Ask and ye shall receive,' is an old scriptural saying we often hear quoted. The farmers have been asking, the market-gardeners have been asking, but this government, instead of giving them bread, are giving them a stone.

Now are they not entitled to some consideration ? I find that between the farmers and the market-gardeners there are over 412,000 of them in this country. Do their numbers not entitle them to some cor [DOT] sideration ? AVe have given protection tc the manufacturer, we are paying a bounty to those who are producing iron, we are paying a bounty to those who are manufacturing binder twine, and to several other 'lines. But the 'great agricultural class of the country, the mainstay of the country to-day, can knock at the door of parliament in vain, because the gentlemen who control the destiny of this country for the time being are opposed to giving them protection, and are in favour of the principle of free trade. The hon. member for Brant has voiced their sentiments to-night,

so has the hon. member for Gasp6 (Mr. Lemieux) ; and the premier himself has devoted hut one minute to their interest and that is all. The premier says : We can give you no consolation, because the budget speech is coming down next week,-and he thinks this debate is sprung at an inopportune time. Why, this is the very best time of all others to bring it on. We are bringing this question up in time so as to draw the attention of the government to it, we want to bring before the government the needs of the market-gardeners and the farmers before the Finance Minister makes his pronouncement, then there will be no excuse for the government if they do not give that relief these people require.

If the inspections are made daily, and the average is taken in that way, we get a fair idea of the purity or illuminating power of the gas in any one factory or city ; but if the inspection is taken only once a month or now and again, it might happen to be taken in a certain city on a day when the gas was poor, and so a false idea would be given in regard to its quality. Perhaps the hon. minister would give us an idea of how these inspections are made, how frequently, and under what regulations.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: The regulations were adopted many years ago, and provide that the inspection shall be made as frequently as may be necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: How often would that be ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: It depends entirely on the amount of work the officers have to do in the city where it is done. I shall be glad to send a copy of the regulations to my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I think we should be informed in what way that information is gathered, because I have heard complaints made in gas factories that under the regulations adopted by the department, the public does not get a fair idea of the illuminating power of the gas from the statement issued by the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Has the complaint ever been made to the department ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
Not that I know of.
Mi-. BRODEUR. I never heard any complaint.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I might inform the hon. minister that I found that the gas company in the city which I represent was very low in the scale in regard to the quality of their gas as reported by the Minister of Inland Revenue. maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Scales are manufactured in the United States without being stamped, while scales manufactured in Canada are stamped before they are permitted to be used. Suppose a merchant in Winnipeg imports 100 of these scales, they are sold in Manitoba and the Northwest. What system of inspection does the hon. gentleman apply to them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: As soon as they are imported we are notified by the Customs Department, and then our officers inspect them where they are to be found.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I am informed, and am quite sure that my information is correct, that the law is fulfilled when the importer gives notice to the department that he has a certain number of scales. He can then sell them all over the country, and they are sent 50 or 100 or 200 miles away, and are sold and distributed before the inspector arrives. There are a great many scales used constantly in Manitoba and the Northwest that have had no inspection at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I do not think there are many, because we have assistant inspectors everywhere in the country, and when some scales are imported in that way we are notified of it. and then our inspectors go and inspect them. It was suggested that these scales should be inspected at the Customs Department: but that is not very easy in the case of large scales which have to be set up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: The importer is not allowed to sell them before they are inspected?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: No.	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Did the hon. minister say that if a notice is given the department by the importer of scales, the importer is compelled to hold them until they are inspected ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: That is my impression. He should notify the department right away.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Nevertheless that is not done, and there is nothing in the law to allow the minister to take action against the importers. I make the statement without fear of contradiction that there are imported into the Territories and Manitoba at present scales that are not stamped, and when the importer notifies the department that he has imported those scales, he has complied with the law and may sell them [DOT]before they are inspected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I have had no such case brought to my knowledge. I would be very glad if my hon. friend could give me Instances where the law has been violated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I think I understood the minister to say that it would be very in-1 convenient to inspect them at places where they were stored, as they could not be set up in those places. Very often the scales are large and have to be removed to the places where they are going to be established and set up before they can be inspected. That confirms the statement of my hon. friend from Peel, who says that the law is complied with when notice is given the department by the importer, and that the importer is then at liberty to sell. Does the minister not know what the regulations are in the matter ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: The regulations provide that when a scale is imported we should be notified, and then an officer is *

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: sent to inspect it. Perhaps the law is defective. Perhaps the hon. member for Peel is referring to a case brought to my knowledge the other day of somebody in the west who claimed to have notified the department that he had a scale and no inspector went up there for some time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: If the regulations order the importer to notify the department, then' as a matter of course the minister should see that the scales are inspected. But if the regulations do not provide against the selling of the scales before inspection, would it not follow that when the importer had given the notice, he would have done all required and could go on selling at once ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: The point is this : Suppose a merchant in Brandon imports 100 scales from Chicago. When they have passed through the customs house and are in his store, he notifies the department that they are ready for inspection. He has then complied with the law and begins at once to sell them. They will be sold and scattered for hundreds of miles all over the Territories and Manitoba before they are inspected. I say that the minister should change the law by providing that the scales could not be sold until they are inspected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: The regulations provide that all manufacturers and importers should notify the district inspector of the shipments and destinations of all weighing machines which cannot be inspected until finally set up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: That just carries out what I have said. The importer complies with the law when he gives notice that the scales are in his place and then may go on selling them. The law should be altered so that he would not be permitted to sell them until they are inspected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Perhaps the law is not suflicient to cover the case, and I will see that Mr. Pike looks into the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: No doubt wTe should not permit the importation and use of those scales, and I am sure that my officers absolutely. refuse to inspect them. In some cases I think we ordered that they should be re-exported.	,

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Where were those ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I think in the west.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: , No scale can be used unless registered. The scale has to be inspected and stamped before you can use it. Scales coming into Canada, if not stamped, are rejected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: My hon. friend from Peel says that if inspections are made before the scales are sold by the importer, the customs would have control and the work be done satisfactorily ; but in one case 100 scales were purchased, and without having been inspected or adjusted they were sob and are being used. This is a very serious matter, especially if the statement can be made good that an inducement is held out to the dealers by advertising that these scales are so unfair and fraudulent that the consumer is not getting what he pays for. It is a very serious matter, especially in the sparsely settled districts if fraudulent scales are permitted to pass from the importer to the retailer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Perhaps we could inspect these scales at the customs office ; but, as I said a minute ago, I suggested this myself and X was told that it could not be very easily done. And if it is found that these scales are not in accordance with oul' laws the parties receive instructions to re-export them.	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I agree with the minister on that point. But how is the inspector to find out where the scales are, if they are sold to different men using them in distant parts of the country ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Our inspectors go everywhere throughout the country and find these scales. And, if the scales are not right they are destroyed or re-exported. I am sure that in one case, at least, that has been done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman will not say that his inspectors can go to every farm house all over Canad_a to test the scales. That is not their duty. Or, perhaps I may be wrong in that ; but, I understand that "they only inspect scales used by merchants.
Mr. BRODEUR, If a man uses scales only for himself we do not care much. The Weights and Measures Act is made specially for the protection of the public. We inspect every two years the scales that are in use by dealers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROTECTION FOR FARM AND GARDEN PRODUCTS.

It seems to me that the suggestion of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) is a good one and would expedite business-that those scales should be inspected before they are distributed.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to ask the government whether or not they have taken any steps with regard to the strike inaugurated at the works of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company at Sydney, in my province ? As the government is no doubt aware, the works of this company are of the greatest possible importance to the town of Sydney, which is now a large community of some 12,000 or 14,000 people, although ten or twelve years ago it was a village of only 2,000 or 3,000 population. The interests of the town and of the people who reside there are bound up very largely in the prosperity of this company, and of the Dominion Coal Company. I understand from pres* reports that about 1,800 men have gone on strike and that the works of the company are closed down, and are likely to be closed down for an indefinite period. This would seem to be a special occasion when the intervention of the government is demanded ; the results of this strike may be that five or six thousand people will leave the province of Nova Scotia and endeavour to find homes in the United States.
It is therefore of the utmost possible importance that everything in the power of the government should be done for the purpose of bringing the strike to an end and of causing the company to resume its operations. I do not know whether the government has taken any steps tending towards intervention, but I have been informed that the Board of Trade of Sydney has sent a communication to the government by telegraph, asking that some such steps be taken. My information did not come from the board of trade itself, but from another quarter, and I thought it a sufficiently important matter to bring to the attention of the government at once. I should be glad if the right hon. gentleman, in the absence of the Minister of Labour, would give the House any information as to what the government has done or what it proposes to do, with respect to a matter of such very great importance, not only to the interests of Sydney, but to the whole province of Nova Scotia, and I may say to the whole Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 join-with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in recognizing the very great importance of the matter to which ho ha3 referred, and I assure the House that if, by the intervention of the Minister of Labour or in any other way, the government, by the exercise of its friendly offices, can bring about a better understanding between the company and the workmen, it will be both our duty and our pleasure to do so. The strike, as the hon. gentleman has intimated, is one of recent hours, and has only now taken definite effect. The communication to which he has referred has been received by the Department of Labour, and the matter is now engaging the minister's attention, it is not possible at the present moment to indicate in what way the Department of Labour or the government may intervene ; but I assure the hon. gentleman that we appreciate the importance of the matter, and we shall be glad to do anything we can, by friendly intervention or in any other way, to bring about a solution of the difficulty.

Rill (No. 100) to amend the Pilotage Act.- (Mr. Prfifontaine) was read the second time and House went into Committee thereon.

The Bill is very short as hon. gentlemen will see. Last year a Bill was introduced placing the pilots between Montreal and Quebec under the authority of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It was done at the request of the pilots, the boards of trade and the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal and Quebec. In the Bill there was a clause by which the district of Saguenay was'put under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as regards pilotage, but the Bill did not go far enough in conferring authority on the Minister of Marine to control entirely the pilotage of the Saguenay river, and when it became necessary to prepare rules for the pilotage of the Saguenay river, we considered that we had not sufficient powers. A commission was appointed in Chicoutimi to supervise the pilotage of the river, but the authority of the pilotage itself does not reside in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and we think it is in the interest of navigation that it should be. petent to judge of the case, to investigate the matter, and to decide whether the pilot who is accused has made himself liable to punishment under the law. Now I leave it to my hon. friend himself. I do not quite agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) who has just taken his seat. In interpreting this Bill he seems to think that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will be placed in the position of being the sole judge. The hon. gentleman knows that the pilotage authorities in Montreal and Quebec consult with some of the pilots. Will my hon. friend (Mr. Geoffrion) allow me ? My hon. friend is absolutely astray iii so far as the pilotage district of Quebec is concerned. The board is composed by law of the harbour commissioners of Quebec and the president of the pilots is one of the members of the board. The composition of the board is fixed by law and you cannot take in any more pilots.
Very well, but does the hon. gentleman pretend that they have not the right to consult any of the pilots?
Decidedly I do say so.

I have known instances in Montreal and Quebec where they have consulted three or four of the pilots. The pilotage authority is frequently composed of men who have no experience whatever. They are merchants in Quebec and they generally consult with pilots, with men of experience and with lawyers ? I think it is proper that the authority in regard to pilotage should be vested in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If anything important occurs is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries not the proper person to see that a remedy is provided ? In the same way if anything goes wrong in the courts in any province of the Dominion, the Minister of Justice sees that a proper remedy is provided.

The analogy which my hon. friend (Mr. Geoffrion) suggests works out in this way that if you brought all the courts of the country under the authority of the Minster of Justice he would try everything himself ?

Not at all. I understand that this Bill means that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will be the authority to whom we shall apply if any of the boards, at Quebec, Halifax. St. John and Montreal are doing anything wrong.
He has the right himself to try cases. He supersedes the boards.

Yes, but he has the power to consult with the boards themselves. He has the right to consult the pilots just the same as the boards have. That is the way I understand the Bill. It reads as follows :
Notwithstanding anything in the Pilotage Act, the Governor in Council may, when it appears to him to be in the interest of navigation, appoint the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to be the pilotage authority for any pilotage district, or for any part thereof ; and the minister shall thereupon supersede the then existing pilotage authority for that district or part of a district.
Does it really mean that the minister shall be himself the pilotage authority sitting as a judicial authority ?
Yes.
Yes.
He is over every person ?
No.

The functions of the pilotage authorities in Quebec and Montreal are divided. In addition to the pilotage authority they have judicial powers. Perhaps I am not interpreting this Bill as it should be interpreted, but I think that the hon. minister by this Bill does not take it upon himself to sit alone as a judicial authority.
Mr. TALBO'T. In answer to the objections that my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) has raised against the actual proposition of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries I may tell my hon. friend from Montmorency that I am somewhat interested in this Bill from the fact that a great number of the pilots of Quebec live in my county.
How many V

The only objection that the pilots of Quebec have to the change of authority is. and I had a conversation with the president yesterday about it-he was in Ottawa-that under the new authority probably the pilots of Quebec will not be treated with so much leniency as they are now. That is their only fear. I do not think my hon. friend can name one member of the harbour commission of Quebec outside of the president of the corporation of pilots, who is an ex-officio member of the board, who knows anything about pilotage or about the river St. Lawrence.

I do not know how it is in Quebec, but in the maritime provinces I think the boards are composed partly of merchants and partly of men who have practical experience. I can recall that at the present time at least, two men, perhaps three, on the board of pilot commissioners in Halifax are retired master mariners of great experience. X think this is a practice which prevails in the lower provinces almost universally. But. referring for a moment to the observations of my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Geoffrion) I wish to say that it does not seem to me that there can be any doubt as to the meaning of this amendment.
The Governor in Council may, when it ap-pejrs to him to he in the interest of navigation, appoint the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to be the pilotage authority for any pilotage district, or for any part thereof ; and the minister shall thereupon supersede the then existing pilotage authority for that district or part of a district.
Can there be any doubt about the meaning of that ? The pilotage authority has functions of different characters. It lias administrative functions ; it has judicial functions. In respect to every function it can exercise under the law it is to be superseded by the minister under the terms of this statute. I do not think my hon. friend will disagree with that proposition. I do not see how he can disagree. Is that a wise provision to make in regard to every pilotage authority throughout Canada ? My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has made an argument about one pilotage district-the Saguenay district-about which I profess to know very little, but as to the other pilotage authorities in Canada we have heard no word from the hon. gentleman beyond this that he says he is taking this power as a matter of precaution because these pilotage authorities may make some rules or regulations that are not wise, or that they may refuse to carry out rules and regulations that have Been made and approved and that are wise and should be carried out. In the first place, as far as the rules and regulations are concerned, my distinct recollection of the Pilotage Act is. that these rules and regulations must be approved by the Governor in Council or by the department-I think by the Governor in Council
By the Governor in Council.

Before they have any force whatever. Therefore, in that respect the public are amply safeguarded by that provision. In so far ns the other part of the hon. gentleman's argument is concerned. namely, that, the pilotage authorities may not carry out the law. the Governor in Council has ample authority if they do not carry out the law. The Governor in Council can dismiss them and ap-

point others in their places. He can call upon them, in the first place, to carry out the law and if they refuse he can take either one or other of these remedies. Therefore, there does not seem to me to be any occasion for the enactment of a law of this character and I do not think the hon. minister professes to have given any reason for the enactment of the proposed amendment except in so far as it may have application to the Saguenay district as to which I do not profess to have any information because I do not know what the facts may be.

The Bill will only have application where it is necessary to apply it. The board of the port of Montreal last year, with the consent of the business people, the shipping interests, the harbour commissioners and the pilots came here last year and got this Act put through parliament. Chapter 48, 3 Edward VII., vests the pilotage authority of Montreal in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If the business people of Montreal believe that such a law should be passed, surely their opinion must be of some value. The business people of Quebec have insisted that another clause be added to the Bill, so as to take from the pilotage authority <jf the district of Quebec the supervision of the Saguenay river. The reason they give is, that some of the pilots that have been assigned to the Saguenay were absolutely in-comxietent. Let me ask : is the country not generally interested in having the law applied in' such a way as to offer the necessary guarantees for safe navigation ? Why should not authority be given to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to act as a pilotage authority ? The great objection raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) is that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will subsitute himself for the pilotage authority, and for the men who formerly held this investigation, but the hon. gentleman loses sight of chapter 64. the Act of 1901, under which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has authority to hold investigations and to delegate his powers.
There is nothing about the pilots in that Act.
It makes no difference whether the pilot is tried under the Shipping Casualties Act, or by men chosen by the harbour commissioners of Quebec or St. John or elsewhere.
The difference is that a pilot cannot be tried under the Act to which the minister has referred.
The investigation takes place under that Act, and everything is done to ascertain who is responsible for the accident.
It has nothing at all to do with the pilots.

Surely it is in tlie interests of the country, that pilots should pass such an examination under proper authority, as will guarantee that they are capable of discharging their duties. I do not see what harm there is in the pilotage authority being put in the hands of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Indeed I believe it will afford better protection to the shipping interests.

My hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) has said that one of the reasons why some of the pilots are opposed to this Bill, is that the new pilotage authority would not be so lenient as the existing body. Well, I have had considerable experience in practising before these pilotage courts ; I have been the solicitor for the pilots for the last twenty years, and I know that the complaint is not that the pilotage authority in Quebec is too lenient, but rather quite the reverse. The pilotage authority in the district of Quebec is composed of nominees of the government-and the government should appoint men who know something about the business-and also of a number of gentlemen who are elected by the shipping interests of Quebec. For the most part these gentlemen know a good deal about shipping ; some of them know a good deal about navigation, and they are competent to try such eases as come before them. In addition to that, they have the president of the Corporation of Pilots to throw light upon any question on which they are adjudicating. Let me point out that the Minister of Marine, who is not yet the lord high admiral of the Canadian navy does not know much about navigation, and although he has taken several trips on the ' Eureka ' and the * Frontenac,' he is not by any means a past master in the science of navigation. For my part, I would be loath to go before him with a trial in which a pilot was accused of neglect in navigating his ship. The Minister of Marine is not only not a fresh water sailor even, but he is not a sailor at all, and if the existing pilotage authority in Quebec is not competent to try these cases, surely the Minister of Marine cannot set up a claim to competency. The minister quoted the Shipping Casualties Act of 1901, but it ought be needless to tell him that that Act has nothing to do with pilots at all. The Act is simply for the purpose of instituting inquiries and investigations into shipping casualties, to determine whether the master, or the engineer, or one of the officers of the ship has been guilty of any neglect or error in navigation. The law respecting pilots provides how they shall be tried and their trial is a very serious matter. It is held as in a court; counsel represent the pilots and the government, evidence is taken under oath and the proceedings are just the same as in any court of the land. It is so serious that the law 130
has allowed an appeal to the Superior Court on any decision rendered by the pilotage authority. The offences which a pilot may be guilty of range all the way from being intoxicated while on duty, to stranding a ship, and the penalty is a minimum of $20 fine up to the taking away of the pilot's license during his lifetime. '
My hon. friend should limit the Bill to the interpretation which he put upon it when he gave the explanations to the committee. We on this side of the House, I particularly, have no intention of doing anything which would be contrary to the wishes of the business men of Montreal or Quebec ; but it cannot be their wish to vest in my hon. friend, the political head of a department, the powers which the Revised Statutes of Canada give to the pilotage authorities, that is, the trial of offences of which the pilots may be charged. I would, therefore, move .
That the following words be added at the end of section 1 :-
Provided that nothing in this Act shall empower or authorize the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to sit as a tribunal for the trial of offences of which pilots may be accused before the pilotage authorities.

I have no objection at all to the amendment, because it has never been my intention to sit as a tribunal in these cases. The minister is incompetent to do so ; besides, in cases involving the cancellation of the certificate, there are always assessors appointed who are mor'e competent to act.

speakeroldname: Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: This Bill is a very short one. and its object is to remedy an unsatisfactory state of affairs which exists on the lakes. Some years ago, I think it was in 1890, some international rules were adopted at a meeting that took place in Belgium, at which marine interests all over the world were represented, and by which certain rules were drawn up and adopted as the rules of navigation. However, the Americans navigating on the lakes did not conform to these rules, they have maintained their own rules since then, and in consequence a good deal of misunderstanding has been created amongst navigators on the lakes. The Marine Association 'has come to the conclusion that it would be better to agree with the Americans and adopt the same rules they have as regards that portion of our inland waters. This Bill is a result of the representations made by the Canadian Marine Association.
I think the object of the Bill is very good. But I would ask my hon. friend to point out by whom the regulations mentioned in this subsection which he desires to add to the Act, were passed.
By the Governor in Council under chap. 79 of 49 Yic.

Well, we consulted the Department of Justice on the question, and the opinion of the department was to the effect that it would be better to have a special law, to get special authorization by statute to amend these regulations. Because by section 14 of chap. 79, 49 Yic., it is provided :
If Her Majesty, acting on the joint recommendation of the admiralty and the Board of Trade, hy Order in Council annuls or modifies any of the regulations for preventing collisions on navigable waters, which, by order of Her Majesty in Council of the fourteenth day of August, 1879, were substituted for those heretofore in force for like purposes in the United Kingdom, or makes new regulations in addition thereto or in substitution therefor, the Governor in Council may, from time to time, make corresponding changes as respects Canadian waters, in the regulations contained in the second section of this Act or any that may be substituted for them,-or may suspend them or any of them, and make others in their stead,-or may revise all or any of the regulations in the Act of the parliament of Canada passed in the thirty-first year of Her Majesty's reign, and intituled ' An Act respecting the Navigation of Canadian Waters,' as he deems best for ensuring the correspondence of the. regulations of Her Majesty in Council with those of the Governor in Council.

I may be mistaken, but from bearing what the hon. gentleman has just read, I should think that this Bill was not necessary. I do not know whether we should spend any time here passing useless legislation. But really it seems to me, from the language of this section 14 that the Governor in Council have a right to change any regulations which have been heretofore, in existence, to alter, amend or supersede them by other regulations. I may be mistaken, but that seems to me to be the meaning of section 14.

There seems to be a doubt whether we can amend these regulations, unless they are made to correspond with the rules and regulations adopted by the Admiralty and the Imperial Board of Trade. So in order to make the law perfects clear, we thought it would be better to insert a special clause providing that, even if they do not agree with the regulations made by the admiralty, these rules may be passed. Besides, they are perfectly independent of the others.

He says that there are members who make long speeches that fill columns and columns of * Hansard ' when there are only six members present and three of them asleep. He continues :
Such a member, said Mr. O'Donoghue, had no more effect than a dog has when he sits on his hind legs and barks at the moon. But when a member is regarded with respect by his fellow members rises the scene was different. The side door is opened and the members flow in from all quarters of the House to listen to that man. I was in the House of Commons one day and Smith rose to speak. The House was almost empty at the time, but in a few moments every member within the precincts of the House was in his place. The premier and cabinet ministers who were sitting partly with their backs to Mr. Smith turned half around and with all the others were all attention to the words that fell from the lips of your representative and ours. Here was Mr. O'Donoghue, an official of the government who was supposed to take no part in politics, speaking on the hustings in favour of a government supporter. Yours very truly,

* I may say that if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) had given me any notice yesterday of his intention to bring before the House certain statements that I had made the *day before in connection with remarks that he had made about the hon. member for Lennox, I would not have considered the matter of sufficient importance to bring it before the House to-day. The question of the veracity of the statements made by hon. gentlemen on either side of this House is a very important and serious matter, and X take it that hon. gentlemen on the government side of the House will be as eager as lion, gentlemen on this side to uphold any hon. gentleman in this House who rises in his place and makes a statement of fact or a statement that he believes to be a statement of fact. I am sure that if any hon. gentleman so far forgets himself as to rise in his place simply for the purpose of interrupting an hon. gentleman and thereby gaining some party advantage for the moment by reason of an untruthful statement, such conduct on either side of the House should be condemned. That I take it is the disposition of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) in his effort the day before yesterday to make a point against the leader of the opposition who was then discussing the question of immigration alluded to the fact that the leader of the opposition wa s using exactly the same language that he himself had used in a debate that occurred one year previous to that. He said that he used the same observations somewhat on the same line as the hon. leader of the opposition and that they were condemned by my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson). My hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) rose in his place and contradicted that statement, and I desire to give the contradiction, as X shall give the statement made by the junior member for Halifax, because I think this matter is of sufficient importance to be placed on record. The hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) made this statement :
Mr. Speaker,, you will remember that about this time last year there was a debate in this House on this very subject. On that occasion I made some observations somewhat in the line of the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition this afternoon. I was taken to task on that occasion by my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) who denied to a considerable extent the statements I made.
Then the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) rose in his place and replied as follows :

Will the hon. member allow me to correct him. Instead of my making a speech after him, he spoke after I did and criticised me.
Now I take it that the object of my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) in correcting the hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) was to show that he had not made statements making any allusion to the hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) by which he had controverted statements that that hon. gentleman had made. Now any hon. gentleman in this XIouse after an interruption of that kind would have accepted the statement made by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) as be is bound to do as a member, of this House. But what did he do instead. He replied by saying :
I am quite aware that my hon. friend, like a great many others in the House, after he has made the principal speech generally makes a few little speechlets.
What was the object in saying that ? It was that if the leading speech of my hon. friend did not contain these remarks that controverted the statement of the hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) the contradictions could be found in the speechlets. I had the record in my hands then as I have it now'. I rose in my place and I did not speak offensively. I used perfect parliamentary language in so far as I am able to express it and I said this :
I would remind the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) that he is mistaken when he thinks that the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) followed him last year with a speech or even with a speechlet.
Meaning by that that neither the speech nor the speechlets contained any remark that in any wray controverted anything that had been said by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche), and I continued :
There is no record of either such speech or speechlet, hut I can tell him that the hon. gentleman who did follow' him and who criti-

cised his language very severely was the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver.)
Then the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) made this statement:
Speaking from memory I thihli my hon. friend did make the few observations I referred to or else it was the gentleman next him. I am not speaking by the book of course but from memory. The statement I made certainly was attacked afterwards by my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver).
Now Sir, I am in duty bound, Mr. Speaker, having '.corrected the hon. gentleman to prove by the record that the statement I make in connection with the language used by my hon. friend is correct. We were discussing on July 14, 1903, a motion moved by the Hon. Mr. Sifton, Minister of the Interior :
That the House again go into Committee of Supply.
That is reported on page 6546 of the * Hansard ' of 1903. Mr. Wilson, if I may use his name, occupied the pages of ' Hansard ' from 6546 down to 6557 when Mr. Roche, the junior member for Halifax followed him. I see that this speech of Mr. Roche continues to page 6562. Twelve hon. gentlemen in this House spoke on that occasion after the junior member for Halifax and before we find a page with Mr. Wilson's name and previous to his remarks the' Hon. Mr. Sifton makes this statement at page 6609 :
The only persons we hear that suggestion from is the hon. member for Lennox and his friend the United States inspector, Mr. Watchorn. if my understanding of the hon. gentleman's argument is correct, it is in effect that we should make such an arrangement as would allow the officers of the United States to decide who should come into Canada.
M.\ WILSON. 1 made no such statement. What I said was that we ought to enter into an arrangement with them, that we ought to have as much to say about it as the Americans, aud that there should be a good understanding between the w o governments.
I wish to point out to you that there is not one statement in these words which refers in any way to the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche). Again Mr. Sifton says :
A medical inspector is stationed at each of the ports of landing, a competent medical inspect". They are all presided over by a general inspector of first-class professional attainments ; and we have no reason whatever to believe that it is necessary that their inspection should he revised by officers of the United States.
When was the medical inspector appointed at Montreal ?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the date.
I may say that his deputy minister was before the committee as late as the 11th of June, and, according to his evidence, no one had been appointed there then.

The hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) uttered nothing further up to the time the motion to go into supply was carried. Then the item of immigration, $110,000 was taken up for discussion. The hon. member for Lennox was discussing the item with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). He spoke several times, making what the hon. junior member for Halifax call ' speechlets.' But in none of them is there a reference to the junior member for Halifax or to the arguments which he says the hon. gentleman controverted. The debate on the main motion and on the item of $110,000 was closed at page 6616 :

Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.20 a.m. Wednesday.
Now, I wish to say and say it most positively that In the record I have quoted there is no contradiction of the statement made by the junior member for Halifax. 1 have here the volume of * Hansard ' containing 2429 pages between June 22nd and July 29th, 1903 ; and, Mr. Speaker, I will apologize to this House if the junior member for Halifax can put his finger on a single word or syllable in the debate' on this question in which the hon. member for Lennox controverted the statements he made as coming from the junior member for Halifax. What I wish to point out is this- that the junior member for Halifax, after having twenty-four hours to consider what he wished to say, came to this House yesterday and, without extending to me the courtesy that I have extended to him, brought up without a moment's notice, and without even having before him the record to prove his statement, this matter to which he had previously referred. I read from the report :

I rise for the purpose of making a personal explanation. Yesterday, in the course of the debate, I stated that the hon. member for Lennox had controverted some remarks *which I had made. He said that he could'nt have done so, because he had spoken before me. I then said that that gentleman like some others in the House, after he had made his main speech, added a number of little speeches or speechlets.
Though the member for Lennox made certain speechlets, three before the motion carried, yet they had no bearing on the statements made by the hon. junior member for Halifax. No hon. gentleman on either side of the House would say that the junior member for Halifax strengthened his case by proving that the member for Lennox spoke when w-hat he said had nothing to do with the matter under discussion. He says, later on :
Now, my reputation being assailed and I have been directly contradicted without warrant, an explanation is due from the hon.

member (Mr. Ingram), and it that is the | method in which he pursues investigation, then if he contradicts me on some future occasion, he had better have his facts more under control of his volition.

I still adhere to the statement I made yesterday, and the record will prove my statement to be correct. The Jion. gentleman from Lennox was afterwards' speaking on an item in the estimates, which affected the question of immigration.
It was the same debate on his motion, and he afterwards reaffirmed his previous statement.

The record will prove that the statement I made yesterday was correct, and if the record does not prove that, I am willing to apologize. I defy the hon. gentleman from Halifax (Mr. Roche) to read from the record exactly the statements made by the hon. gentleman from Lennox.
My hon. friend said that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) made neither speech or speechlet, but the record shows that he made eight speeches.
Read.

I have not the book here ; the gentlemen on the other side of the House have it.
Now, I do not wish to detain the House longer on this question.
Hear, hear.

Do hon. gentlemen opposite dispute my statements in connection with this matter ? They cheered the junior member for Halifax when he made his statement. And I challenge any mem. her on the other side of the House, the junior member for Halifax included, to say that the record I have quoted is not correct. I have been a member of this House for a number of years, and I challenge any member on either side to put his finger on a single line of the record showing that I have ever interrupted any hon. gentleman for the purpose of making light of him and knowing that what I said was not in accordance with the facts. So, I am only giving to this matter the importance it deserves. I have not heen guilty of the conduct in debate that has been suggested, and God forbid that I should ever be guilty of it. But it appears that the hon. junior member for Halifax, unable to gain importance in this House in any other way, resorts to tactics of this kind in order to have a fling at his colleague (Mr. R. L. Borden) who is the honoured leader of the opposition. He must devise some other means, and he better acquainted with his facts when he rises to speak in this House. For my part, I condemn conduct of this kind. Had it not been for tbe request of my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) who had already spoken and so could not speak again, I do not think I would have paid any attention to the statement of the junior member for Halifax. But, having made my statement I stand by it and I appeal to tbe records to support me.

When the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) was speaking on the occasion to which he referred, I interrupted him because I thought he was mistaken, that he had forgotten that I had spoken before him. He wished for some member from the west to corroborate his statement. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) followed him and I do not think he enjoyed very much the support he got from that hon. gentleman. Now I have taken the pains since this came up-though I may say, that had it ended with the first day I would have thought nothing more about it-to look over what the hon. gentleman said, to see if I had interrupted him during the debate. I substantiate everything that the hon. member from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has said. The hon. member (Mr. Roche) will fail to find that I interrupted his speech or made any reference to what he said. I have no fault to find with the hon. gentleman as a good citizen or as a pleasant member of this House ; hut he is noted more for being a little windy than for familiarity with subjects that he undertakes to deal with in debate. Now, I have never said so much about any man in this House. I desire to discuss matters on their merits and not to deal in personalities, because I think that is unwise and entirely uncalled for. As to the opinion the hon. gentleman expresses on the question of immigration, one has only to read the papers of to-day to see that we are getting a most undesirable class from abroad, people who are becoming a burden on a number of our cities. I think the time has come for the government to exercise the power it possesses to keep out this class of people. We all are enthusiastic believers in the capabilities of our country, and our population, up to this time, has been equal, I believe, to that of any other country in manliness, honesty, industry and the other great virtues. I hope the government will not allow outsiders to enter and become citizens who will he an undesirable addition to our population. This is all I want, and I think I am speaking the opinion of our friends on this side of the House. We are quite satisfied to get as large a population as possible into this country if it is of a desirable kind. But what we want especially is population of a good quality, we are not so anxious about the quantity as about the quality. I have only further to say, Mr. Speaker, that I think in this matter the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) is entirely mistaken, and if he is not wilfully mistaken, he certainly should not have spoken in the way he did without information.

Motion agreed to, and House went into-Committee of Supply.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.

Adulteration of food and fertilizers, and .the administration of the Act respecting fraudulent marking, $30,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speechtext: I suppose it is not necessary for me to give full information on an item that we discussed the other night. This is a provision for carrying out the Act concerning the Adulteration of Pood, to pay food inspectors and analysts. The vote is the same as last year.
Was there fraudulent marking of food in Canada to any extent last year ?
I am informed by my [DOT]deputy that there has been a decrease.
In what classes of goods?
All sorts of foods, maple syrup, jellies, pepper, distilled liquors, &c. I may say that the beverage which seemed on the whole to be the purest is the product of the distillery.
I would ask the minister if his officers go around to different places, or if samples are sent here to be analysed ?

We have food inspectors who travel around the country to gather samples, and they are sent to be analysed. The inspectors are obliged to go all through the country and collect samples. They collect samples without acting upon any information given them.
I understand that would be their general duty, but I presume if they had information from any particular locality that adulterated food was being sold he would send his officers.
Certainly, if we had information from any locality that impure food was being sold, it would be the duty of the department to send inspectors to collect samples of such food, and that would be done.
How much was expended last year ?

$19,841.3S were expended last year.
Minor revenues, $1,000 ; ordnance lands, $1,080.

The vote for minor revenues is to pay some expenses in connection with granting licenses to ferries between the provinces and between the United States and Canada on the lakes. The Department of Inland Revenue is charged with that duty, and we have to, advertise for this purpose. I may say that the revenue collected from ferries is much larger than the amount we spend.
By what principle do these come under the Inland Revenue Department ?

They have always been under the control of the Inland Revenue Department. There are two departments charged with the collection of revenue, the Customs and the Inland Revenue, and as ferries yield a revenue they are given to my department.
How much was collected last year ?
The ferries are not totalled up, but the collections are divided into three parts-bridges, ferries and sundries, and the total sum is $1,239.50.
How much have you to pay out of that in the way of expenses ?

The expenditure for the ferries is not totalled up, but an expenditure has been made as follows : American Bank Note Company for printing Yukon stamps, $766, and for printing law stamps, 8020.30, and then there were some express charges and some expense in connection with the advertising for tenders, which amount to about $50.
When you gave us the revenue you gave us the bridges as well as the ferries. What is the expense in connection with the bridges ?

I do not see any expense in so far as the bridges are concerned. The expense seems to be entirely in regard to the following ferries between Gower Point and Lapasse, the Quyon ferry, the ferry between Hawkesbuury and Grenville and the ferry between Cross Point and Campbellton. There are no expenses in connection with the bridges.-. We have simply collected money without having spent anything.
You received some $1,200 and you expended more than you got.
No, my hon. friend is mistaken.
I understand you gave an amount of $1,239 as the revenue ? You have given $766, $020 and $50 as the expenditure which would make over $1,400.
This amount of $766 has not been spenc on the ferries. It has been spent for Yukon law stamps. It has been charged to this vote, but it has not been spent for advertising in regard to the ferries.

How would an ordinary man looking at the accounts be able to tell what this expenditure is for ? I think the accounts should be kept in such a way that any ordinary man going through the Blue-book would be able to tell what the revenue is taken from, and what it has been spent for.

If my hon. friend will look at page K-25 of the Auditor General's Report, he will see everything explained there :
Minor revenues-expenditure, $1,507.81.
Out of that the sum lfl.394.3S has been spent for law and mining court stamps in the Yukon. We spent about $200 for advertising ferry leases and we have $1,200 of revenue, so that we are on the safe side.
Arts, agriculture and statistics-exhibitions, $200,000. ,
What is the increase of $50,000 for ?

This item covers all the work of the department for exhibition purposes. The vote of $150,000 for the current year was devoted to the closing up of some slight accounts left over and to paying up to the 1st of July next of the expenses in connection with the St. I,ouis exhibition. The item of $200,000 that is asked for the ensuing year, is estimated on the basis of finishing iip everything connected with the St. Louis exhibition, which closes on the 1st December next, and then it is expected that there will be about $75,000 left out of this $200,000 to be devoted to future exhibition work. In explanation of that future exhibition work. I may say briefly that the government a little while ago accepted an invitation to take part in a universal exhibition at Liege in Belgium, which commences next spring, and it is also expected that we will take part in one or perhaps two small exhibitions in England for which we have been discussing the means. These exhibitions are of the nature of annual exhibitions, one in London and one in Liverpool. They are special exhibitions devoted to the provision trade. For some time back representations have been made to me that participation in these exhibitions would be of very great advantage to our trade in provisions-butter, cheese, bacon, eggs, flour, wheat and so on. There is to be an exhibition in autumn of this year in London and one in Liverpool, January next. This latter exhibition is rather a new one. but it is one of an important character and one which reaches very largely the trade in that portion of the country which is so densely populated, in South Lancashire. We have decided to take part in a small degree in these exhibitions. and for this reason, I am asking not only the necessary sum to complete the St. Louis exhibition, but also to make pro-vison for our participation in these exhibitions. The two English exhibitions will be commenced and completed within the next fiscal year. The Liege exhibition will continue after the beginning of the following fiscal year, but I think the amount I am asking for will be sufficient to take in that exhibition up to the 1st of July next.
Mr. TAYLOR, Before we open up the question of exhibitions fully, I desire to say that I asked the hon. the Minister of Agriculture the other night a question, and he told me he would make inquires. I pointed out to him that at page D-19 of the Auditor General's Report, there was a record in connection with the Wolverhampton and Cork exhibitions of an expenditure, as follows
Walker, Hiram & 'Sons, 2 cases Canadian whisky, $20.93.
I asked the hon. gentleman whether he purchased this for his own use or for some "of his friends, and he told me that he would have to make inquiries and get the information.

The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that I 'did not purchase it for my own use; the insinuation is unworthy ' of an honourable member. I was not in England ; I had no connection with that exhibition beyond the responsibility as head of the department for the expenditure. I have been informed that this expenditure was made by the commissioner in England on an occasion when there was a large gathering of the journalists of the country, who, before the opening visited the exhibition to inspect it. Apparently this purchase was made for the entertainment of these gentlemen.
Was it one of the exhibits ?
On some occasions we have had to purchase exhibits, but so far as I understand this was not for the purpose of exhibition.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister must recognize that he is responsible for the expenditure.
I said so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I was not aware whether the minister visited this exhibition or not-
No, but the hon. gentleman was perfectly aware that I did not buy whisky for my own personal use.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Whether the hon. gentleman bought it or allowed his officers to buy it, it is all the same. The hon. gentleman came into the government as a representative of the temperance people, and if he allows his officers to purchase a case of Walker & Sons; whisky for the purpose of treating the press or any other representative men, he sinks very low or ought to, in the estimation of the temperance people of Canada. If his officers purchased it without his authority he ought to charge that whisky up to them. Now, in connection *with the Osaka, Japan exhibition, I find in the Auditor General's Report, that there is charged to the Hon. Sydney Fisher : travelling expenses, $1,514.57 ; transport expenses. Canadian Pacific Railway to Japan and re-1 turn, $475.92, total $1,990.49. Then on page

D-26 : Geo. May and Company were paid $40 for a solid leather trunk for the Hon. Sydney Fisher, and then there is a charge of $5.65 for sundries. I understand that the ministers, the same as the members, get solid leather trunks at the opening of each parliament, and this was in the middle of the parliament. I would like the minister to explain this, as well as the $5.65 for sundries. Was it for tips or for other sundries unmentionable or what ? We ought to have a full explanation. In my opinion the government should shut down on these foreign exhibitions. I find that a great deal of this money voted for exhibition purposes is spent in trips for friends. At page D-22 of the Auditor General's Report, we find the following entries : Wm. Hutchison, salary, travelling expenses,*tips, &c., $4,647.72; S. Anderson, salary, travelling expenses, tips, &c., $2,057.80 ; W. A. Burns, salary, travelling expenses, tips, &c., $2,932.07 ; T. K. Doherty, $1,340.54 ; Robt. Hamilton, $2,367.06 ;	W. H. Hay, $2,126.20 ; M.
Hori, $63 ; W. Jamieson, $2,097.75 ; G. Ivamada, $225 ; H. O. Knowlton, $1,768.97. It amounts to a sum of $22,320 on that page, and it is continued on the others. This money appears to be gobbled up by a lot of officers and friends of the ministers who are sent out oni trips to these exhibitions, and I do not know that the country receives any benefit from it. The same state of affairs is going on in St. Louis to-day. There is a wilful waste of money. The minister asked for $150,000 last year and he asks for $50,000 extra this year, making $200,000 in all, and any person who reads the Auditor General's Report and sees how the money is frittered away, must come to the conclusion that Canada receives no benefit from it. If the minister will explain the trunk and tire $5.65, andj this $2,000 expenses for himself in connection with the Japan exhibition, the country will be pleased to know how it was spent.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am just informed that this trunk was secured by my secretary for the purpose of carrying papers, documents and literature which was carried over to Japan with me. I have to assume the full responsibility for it, although I may say that this is the first time I knew anything about it. As to the item of $5.65 for sundries, I do not know just now what they are. Apparently the amount was paid to Geo. May & Co., probably for some repairs or something of that kind, or possibly for a despatch box, but I will find out what it was exactly and let the hon. gentleman know. As to the general question of the expenditure for exhibitions, I venture to say that I am well within the judgment) of the people of Canada when I state that the expenditure made in this connection has been amply repaid to us- in the additional commerce and trade which Mr. TAYLOR.
these exhibitions have brought about, and the credit which has been reflected upon Canada. Many details of this expenditure were entrusted entirely to the officers in charge ; of course as minister I am responsible. I have no hesitation in taking responsibility, because I have chosen men who I believe are competent for this work, and they took charge of it as other officers in my department take charge of the other branches. 1 do not undertake myself to instruct these experienced officers as to the details of their work ; I choose competent men, I give the work into the hands of these competent men, and I assume the responsibility. I am satisfied that their work shall be judged by the results. As to the Osaka exhibition. I explained on my return what the results were. I have heard compliments over and over again as to the good results of that work. The increase of trade between Canada and Japan and the Orient, as the result of that exhibition, is the best testimony of its success. The total expenditure for the Osaka exhibition was $53,000. I venture to say that the prestige which Canada and her products obtained in the Orient, is ample compensation for that expenditure. In addition to that pecuniary return, wre have had opened to us possibilities of future trade which were perhaps unknown before, and W'hich to-day are assured to us if the people of Canada wish to take advantage of them. I cannot at the moment reply any further to the strictures of the hon. gentleman, but I take it for granted that in the course of the discussion other information will be required of me. But I take it for granted that there will be other items on which I will be only too glad to give all the information possible. If I have not now full information. I shall procure it and lay it before the House, because there is nothing in the whole matter which will not redound to the credit of the officers in charge of the exhibitions and of the country.
Mr. TAYLOR, The hon. gentleman says that the expenses in connection with the Osaka, Japan, exhibition amount to $53,000. but according to the Auditor General's Report for 1902-3 there was an expenditure of $59,987.12. Then there is the expenditure for this year, which we have not yet got, because the exhibition is not yet closed. How-does he account for the difference ?

I wmuld ask the hon. minister what increase there has been in the trade between Japan and Canada since his visit to that country, and on what lines ? I would also call his attention to a statement which I understood him to make with regard to these two cases of w-hisky.
1 understood him to say that they had been purchased in England for the representatives of the press, but I find that the purchase w7as made in Canada, and the liquor was taken with him to England.
Are you certain it all readied tliere ?
It was bought from Hiram Walker & Sons and brought to England.
If It reached England, It must have paid the duty or been smuggled in. Surely the hon. minister would not have been guilty of smuggling.
THOMiSON. There is another item, namely, G1 dozen photographs, $30. Are these pictures of the staff given the press ?

This whisky was not bought in Canada but in England. I find that the Walkers have an agency in England, and the whisky was got there. My hon. friend did not quite understand what I said. I told him that we had an entertainment at Wolverhampton before the actual opening of the exhibition, to which the press of Great Britain were invited. I understand that this whisky was bought for that entertainment, and it was bought in England.

In the Auditor General's Report it is entered as Walker & Sons, 2 cases of club whisky. I would infer that it was bought from that firm, whose distillery is in Ontario. The item for photographs is on page D-23, and it says for newspapers. I would imagine that these were the pictures of the staff.
Were they taken before they had this spree or after ?

What was the nature of these papers which were brought over in this $40 trunk ? Are we to understand that the minister's secretary ordered a $40 trunk in which to place some papers, and that the *minister knew nothing about it ?

What I say is that apparently this trunk was ordered by my secretary to take over a large number of papers and documents which I had to take to Japan. As these are heavy articles, he ordered a solid leather trunk at a cost of $40. This is the first time that I have seen the charge, and it seems to me high. I do not think that $40 should be paid for a trunk for any person. The papers consisted of a number of official documents on trade and also literature connected with trade and the country generally.

It seems to me extraordinary that the minister should have a clerk who has so little idea of business procedure that he pays $40 for a trunk and puts some advertising matter into it. What has become of this precious trunk ?
I really cannot say. I suppose it is in the department.

It is amusing to look over these estimates. In one of them I find
that a departmental clerk purchased for himself a fur overcoat. That, however, is not in the hon. gentleman's department. In another case a member of parliament had a fancy writing desk taken to a hotel here, and the country is paying for writing desks for members of parliament, hawked around to their hotels and no doubt taken home with them. It is high time that this thing should be stopped. It is not the amount, but the depth of meanness to which we object ; but evidently some people will descend to anything in order to make a little graft.

There is another strange item in connection with the exhibition at Osaka. 24 pairs of rubbers for women, costing $26, were purchased. This will be seen on page D-24, and further down there are 16 pairs of rubbers for men.
Those were all for exhibition purposes. We bought a rubber exhibit and sent it over there. Amongst other articles were men's and women's rubbers.
What disposition was made of these rubbers ?

They were sold in Japan, and come under the item ' Refund.'
Mr, POPE. Is it customary to buy the exhibits we take to these places ?
We bought all the exhibits that we sent to Osaka.
How much money has been spent on the St. Louis exhibition so far, and what will it cost ?
The total cost up to the 1st of May, 1904, was $107,000.	y

What do you expect the total cost of the exhibition to be ?
Mr. FISHER, I am informed that $325,000 is the total sum.
It is not one-half paid yet ?
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister has not explained how the expenditure has been only $53,000 while the items in the Auditor General's Report total $59,000.

There are items in the Auditor General's Report, which cover the period up to the first of July last year, for nearly $50,000. There is in this years' expenditure a little over $3,000 which makes a total of nearly $63,000. But there is a refund in consequence of the sale of exihibits of nearly $10,000, bringing the net cost down to $53,000 in round figures.
At these foreign exhibitions does the government buy all the foreign exhibits?

In these cases the exhibits belong to the exhibitors ; we did not purchase them, but we aided the exhibitors in making arrangements for the exhibits. There are two reasons. I will take the most important item first. Until this- Japanese exhibition took place Canadian flour was absolutely unknown in the Japanese and Chinese markets.
