I would ask the minister if Canada has an exhibition of live stock at St. Louis, and if not, why not ?

In the first place, the exhibition of live stock at St. Louis does not

begin until next August. In that connection I may make some explanation. There has been a good deal of discussion amongst the breeders in Canada as to the advisability of exhibiting live stock at St. Louis. A deputation came to me last summer and asked that such an exhibit should be made, and asked me to set aside a very large sum, about $120,000, for the purpose of procuring such an exhibit. I felt full sympathy with the breeders of Canada in this regard, because I knew that while some impediments had lately arisen to the sale of our live stock in the United States, still there had been, and is, a large trade, and probably there will be in the future a large trade in thoroughbred live stock with the United States. I therefore discussed the question how we could best secure a creditable exhibit of live stock at St. Louis. While that question was under discussion, certain negotiations took place between my own department and the management of the live stock exhibition at St. Louis. We asked that certain arrangements be made to facilitate the entry of our live stock at that exhibition, that is to say, as to what registration and pedigree of throughbred animals should be recognized as to the various details and conditions of the exhibition. In the course of these negotiations and discussions there was a great deal of correspondence in the agricultural press on both sides of the line, and a good many of our breeders in Canada thought that they would not care to exhibit at all. Not long after the deputation came to see me in Ottawa, I received a letter from one of the leading men in the live stock business in Canada saying that he doubted very much if the very men who asked me to make that arrangement would care to exhibit at all. This came to me as a surprise, and I then took steps to communicate with a number of the live stock breeders in this country. A little while after that the various breeders' associations of Canada, held their meetings in the course of the autumn and early winter, and I think I am speaking correctly when i say that in every one of those meetings of the breeders' associations, discussions arose and resolutions were passed declaring that the associations considered it inadvisable to exhibit live stock at the St. Louis exhibition.
Did they give any reasons ?

Various reasons were given. I do not remember that they were embodied in any of the resolutions sent to me, but I think in some of them they were. The reasons were that they were not satisfied with the conditions which were published, they were not satisfied with regard to the terms upon which Canadian exhibitors could exhibit. I also understood, though I do not know that it was so stated in any of the resolutions, that they were hopeless of a con-131J
tinued market in the United States for their cattle, and especially did they find difficulty in regard to the sale of the animals that were sent to the St. Louis exhibition.
That was the chief complaint ?

One of the chief complaints was that customs regulations of the United States were such that no Canadian animals sent to the St. Louis exhibition could be sold there and left in the country. The breeders did not want to take their animals to St. Louis and go to the expense and trouble of exhibiting them and having to bring them hack. These various resolutions were passed and forwarded to me. I had a great many communications and a great oeal of discussion sometimes with individuals and sometimes through my officers who attended these various meetings of breeders' associations and I found the differences of opinion in regard to the advisability of exhibiting at St. Louis were very great, but what I might call the official or formal (statement of the chief breeders cl this country declared against exhibiting at St. Louis. Then we came to about the middle of winter or early this spring, when I began to receive individual letters from various men saying, that, notwithstanding that the breeders as a body had decided not to show, they individually would like to show and asking what I would do to aid them. I discussed this again with various people with whom I came in contact, and in some letters and I also asked that my live stock commissioner, Mr. Hodgson, should communicate with and meet these people. I have had a very considerable amount of difficulty in determining as to what it was best to do, however, in view of the representations made to me by individuals, I have caused a letter to be prepared to be sent to the different breeders' associations, to individuals who have been communicating with me and to the press, to the effect that while there are differences of opinion and while resolutions have been formally passed by the different breeders' associations it seemed to me to be impossible to secure what I might call a really national, creditable exhibit of live stock at St. Louis ; nevertheless as there seemed to be a considerable number of individuals who wish to exhibit, I would facilitate their exhibition in every way possible, and I would grant to them this pecuniary assistance that I would give to every exhibitor who secures a prize a sum equal to the amount of the prizes that he secures at St. Louis. That is to say that I would double the prizes by granting to every individual securing prizes at St. Louis the 'full amount of the prize he takes. That would be a very considerable help to those who exhibit their stock because I feel confident that anybody who, on his own responsibility, takes animals to St. Louis would take

such good animals and would be so successful that he would get a fair share of the prizes, a larger share of the prizes than would be expected from the number of animals. Therefore, I would supplement the prizes secured by these Canadian exhibitors with an equal amount so as to assist them in paying their expenses. I do not know if the announcement has yet been sent out. but it will be within a day or two if it has not already gone to the press and to the associations.

Independently altogether of the St. Louis exhibition I have had communicat-Mr. FISHER.
ions with Washington as to the difficulties of the customs regulations there, and' I regret to say that we have not had any very great consideration shown to our representations. On the contrary, the Washington customs authorities, I think stimulated by the Department of Agriculture at Washington, have been making their customs regulations more and more stringent all the time instead of relaxing them in any way.

Can the hon. minister give us any idea as to how American exhibitors are treated in Canada, at Toronto, for instance. Last year we held a Dominion exhibition at Toronto and there was a large number of Americans present. Was there any such one-sided arrangement in dealing with the American exhibitors at Toronto as that under which the Canadians are dealt with at St. Louis ?

No, we gave the American exhibitors every facility possible in bringing their animals in here. The Toronto exhibition authorities arranged with the Customs Department to have these animals brought in and to be held in bond. If they were sold here instead of being taken back to the United States every facility was given for such sale. But, our regulations in regard to customs governing the importation of thoroughbred stock and other stock from the United States have never been characterized by the impediments that the regulations of the United States offer to the admission of Canadian stock. I may say in regard to that for the information of the committee, that at a meeting of the live stock breeders of Canada held at the opening of this session, these gentlemen urged very strongly that we should retaliate against the United States, that we should adopt the same regulations in regard to the free entry of thoroughbred animals from the United States that they have adopted towards us. At the present moment my department is busy looking into the question of registration, and the question of what registers and what pedigrees ou.r customs authorities ought to recognize. Heretofore, our customs authorities have been very liberal indeed in recognizing almost any pedigree that was presented to them for an animal claimed to be thoroughbred so as to get free entry under bur customs law. We have not put any impediments in the way. I think we have been too easy in that respect and I know as a matter of fact that certain animals have come into the country free of customs duties which were accompanied by pedigrees which were absolutely worth- ' less for breeding purposes in this country, which would not have been recognized by any breeders' association at all and yet the purchasers thought they were getting animals that were thoroughbred and registered in such a way that

the progeny would afterwards be admitted to register here when, as a matter of fact, they would not be. This is a condition of affairs that ought to be remedied, and one which to-day my live stock commissioner is engaged in studying so as to find out what pedigrees our customs authorities ought to recognize and what they ought to reject. This is a seriously complicated question!, one that presents considerable, difficulties, and one which must be handled with the greatest care so as not to injure the interests of those who have been breeding thoroughbred live stock in this country. It is a question which deserves great consideration, and ought to be dealt with -as soon as possible.

Instead of communicating with the authorities of the exhibition, my opinion is that diplomatic courtesy would have required the Minister of Agriculture to communicate in the first place with the authorities in! Washington. It would appear to me that in these matters, Canadians offer fair and reasonable terms to the American people ; we were willing to reciprocate and are met with retaliation. The minister would be justified in retaliating against such treatment as that. Let us stand on our own dignity. We are just as good as our friends across the border ; we expect fair treatment in return for fair treatment, but if we do not get fair treatment, let us stand on our rights and give them the same treatment as they give us.
This change was made within the past few years?
Yes.

As the United States law now is, an American citizen can come over here and buy thoroughbred Stock and take it back free of duty, but a Canadian is not allowed to send thoroughbred stock into the United States free of duty.
That is it.
Was any remonstrance made by this government when the change was made ? What was the object of the United States government in making such a law ?

I did not ask the reason why they made the law, I may say frankly that the communications I have had of late with the Department of Agriculture at Washington with regard to this matter, have been so unsatisfactory that I have felt it was hardly consonant with the dignity of Canada to make a protest. They told us practically that they were going to regulate their own affairs to suit themselves and they did not care what we thought about it. Some years ago, Mr. Wilson, the United States Secretary of Agriculture, told me in his own office in Washington in so many words :	I believe
that we in the United States have come to the point where we do not want to import any animals from anywhere, and I am not going to do anything to facilitate importations from Canada or from Europe. In view of such a statement I felt that it was not in keeping with the dignity of this country to plead for a relaxation of their arrangements. I feel very much as my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has expressed himself. It is evident that of late years animals have been imported free of duty into Canada, which were not pure bred in the proper sense of the word. Our customs authorities have been in the habit of recognizing anything in the shape of a certificate of registration and to my knowledge many of these certificates are certificates of registration in herd books which are not of any value as to the breed. Many animals have been brought in here as. thoroughbred, Which for all practical purposes were grade animals. Apart from any question of retaliation, it is high time that we should see to the registration which entitles an animal to come in free of duty. When first this matter was discussed with the St. Louis exhibition authorities, they expressed their desire to facilitate our exhibits in every possible way as regards customs arrangements.
What was their proposition ?	_

Their proposition was that the animals should be subject to the ordinary law. My hon. friend (Mr. Gil-mour) is right in saying that within a year [DOT] and a. half, these restrictions have been greatly increasjed; in the United States. Before that, pedigree animals were allowed in free of duty, but the customs authorities made a ruling that an animal could only he sent in free of duty when it was going to be used for breeding purposes by the person importing it. A man in British Columbia sent some horses over the frontier for sale, and he was forced to pay the duty. Shortly afterwards, an amendment was made to the United States customs law which said that only American citizens could import animals for breeding purposes or for sale free of duty, and at the present time no Canadian can take an animal into the United States free of duty and dispose of it there.
There is the chief reason for the Canadian breeders not exhibiting any kind of stock at St. Louis.

That is one of the chief reasons, but there are a number of others as well. The whole question is pretty complicated, and a great many minor difficulties accumulated to bring them to the conclusion to which they seem to have come.
Then there will be no live stock there ?
Yes, there will. A good many individual breeders want to take animals there-horsemen, sheepmen, swine-men, but hardly any cattlemen.

Surely the United States minister at Washington could not have looked np the trade and navigation returns of Canada. If he had, he would have found us in this unfortunate position, that while we exported to the United States 10,432 cattle valued at $292,288, we imported from the United States 37,527 cattle valued at $472,689. Or there was a balance of trade in favour of the Washington Agricultural Department of $180,401. Instead of this government keeping its duty at 20 per cent and allowing American cattle to come in to the extent of $180,401 in excess of the amount we send to the other side of the line. I would ask the hon. minister to use his influence with his colleague the Minister of Finance and try and induce him to raise our duty to 27J per cent. We would then have Canadian and American farmers on an equal footing. Then we would be.advancing a step in the way of protecting our own interests. I could go through the whole list of agricultural products and make the same kind of argument. They do not show much discretion on the other side when they talk about retaliation and as not being willing to reciprocate favours, and I would implore the hon. gentleman to use his influence with the Minister of Finance in order that the latter may give Canadians a fair chance.
The amount of cattle brought from the United States includes settlers' cattle, of which there is a very large number.
That makes no difference.
A large number also are brought from the United States by our ranchmen in western Canada for the purpose of fattening and re-exporting.
To the United States ?

No, to England. Young animals, what are called store cattle, are brought in and fattened or used for breeding purposes and either they or their products are exported to England in fit condition. Some of our ranchmen have gone as far as Mexico and have brought Mexican cattle across through the United States. I have had to put some restrictions on the importation of these for sanitary and quarantine purposes, but have had an earnest protest against any such restriction, Mr. FISHER.
as the ranchmen inform me it is absolutely necessary for their business to import these cattle. These cattle are practically the raw material of our ranchmen.

I am afraid the hon. gentleman is becoming a little bit of a protectionist.
Mi'. FISHER.' No, I have always been in favour of free raw material.	-
The ranchman is a manufacturer of beef the same as any manufacturer is, the manufacturer of agricultural implements.
Quite so.

Does the hon. gentleman pretend to say that these men, who are few in number, are to be encouraged to the detriment of the great class of agriculturists throughout Canada ? Are you going to discourage our cattle raisers by allowing that kind of thing to continue much longer ? If the hon. gentleman will give us the total amount of cattle raised in Canada in 1901, then we will be in a better position to form a conclusion. If the hon. gentleman will raise the duty to 27$ per cent, then let these cattle come in, and we will be able to send cattle into the United States on the same footing.

With regard to dealing with the Americans, I would not retaliate for the mere sake of retaliation, but only on business principles ; and on business principles I do not believe in the importation of young cattle from Mexico and the United States. That import is a source of danger because it may bring in disease. The hon. minister has said that these young cattle are our raw material, but we are raising the raw material in this country to a very large extent, and we ought to protect our own herds that are raising the raw material and encourage them to raise more. And the more we encourage the raising of the raw material in this country, the more rapidly will we bring about that condition of things when we will supply the country further south with the young cattle it requires. I do not at all believe in allowing these little cattle to come from away down south bringing with them Texas ticks, or these little horses bringing in what I need not mention, but what the officers of your department report as dangerous. That is my opinion about retaliation. I believe in dealing with our neighbours on business principles, and on business principles I advise you to look after that business which is going on and which has been going on for two or three years. I want the minister to remember that it is only a very few years since the Americans were up in Manitoba paying such prices for young cattle there that the ranchers in the west could

not meet them. That state of things will come about again. It is not worth while for a short period to allow these young cattle to come in as they have been coming in for the past two or three years. It only sets back the period at which we would meet the demand ourselves, if you allow that raw material to come in in competition with the raw material which you may produce yourself.

When our American friends want to meet a case of that kind they lower the duty to suit their own purposes and then when their purposes are served they raise it again to suit themselves. If they find it to their advantage to lower the duty and then to increase it they do so. They have not a stationary tariff as we have and I would treat them exactly as they treat -us. I do not consider that retaliation at all. Is it not a fair business proposition that if it is good for them after all the years of experience they have had, to adopt this course a similar course must be good for us under like conditions ? We have not yet had the same experience which they have had with the tariff and I think a leaf out of their book in that respect would be a step in the right direction. It is a business transaction not a party transaction.
* Mr. FISHER. I do not want to discuss the tariff to-night. I may however, say that while in no way retaliating or considering what the Americans do, I think we ought to try to regulate our affairs entirely to suit ourselves to protect our interests and to make our people as prosperous as possible. The condition of affairs changes from time to time, as my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mir. Gilmour) said; A few years ago the Americans were buying cattle in Canada and taking them across the lihe because at that time we had not as great a demand in Canada for cattle as they had. My hon. friend knows that those are sent from one part of the country while the others cross the border in another section. Those 10,000 cattle did not go from the Northwest Territories south. In that region the stream is north. These animals went into the eastern states for different purposes and some of them entered at the extreme west. They went to the States because our breeds have been recognized in the United States as being better and notwithstanding all the obstructions and
restrictions whicty the Americans avowedly wish to place on the importation of Canadian thoroughbred stock into the United ' States, we still send a very considerable number of these cattle across the line. Despite all their efforts to shut us out our cattle are so good and the demand for our best cattle amongst the breeders of the United States is so great that they still have to come to Canada for their stock.
Does the hon. gentleman approve of a large number of young cattle coming in from the American ranches'to be placed on Canadian farms ?

If our ranchers find they cannot get supplies sufficient for the interest of their business in Canada I am glad to see that they are enterprising, businesslike and bright enough to get these supplies wherever they can on a profitable basis. If our people in Canada would never go abroad to get anything we would continue to be a small and poor nation.

Would my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture regard it as in the interest of Canada that our duty should be placed high enough to cause the ranchers to breed these cattle in the Dominion of Canada and fatten them in this country rather than to import them ? Do I understand him to say that in his opinion it is better as opportunity presents itself to allow the ranchers of western Canada to purchase their lean small cattle in the United States and to finish them in western Can-anad.
We ship our small cattle into the United States .which are unfit for fattening purposes.

My hon. friend has not a very high opinion of the United States people. United States people have no idea of building up their nation by importing small Canadian cattle into the United States to fatten. That is not the policy of the United States.
They do it ; I do not know their policy but they do it. Cattle unfit for export to England are shipped by hundreds into the United Stats.
What for.
I do not know what for, all I know is that we get American money for Canadian stackers, cattle that we cannot ship to England.
Does my hon. friend think that we cannot keep them here ?
Yearlings and calves and two-year olds have gone in by hundreds ever since the quarantine regulations were removed.

Does my hon. friend think it is a good policy for the Canadian farmer

to breed small cattle and, send them into the United States ?

I do not consider it good policy for a Canadian farmer to sell anything off the farm that cannot walk off, but if he has something which is unfit for him to fatten or to ship to European markets or for which he cannot find a market in Europe, then if he can find a market for it in the United States, I consider it decidedly good policy.
My hon. friend says he does not think it good policy to export anything we can fatten in this country ?
Anything we can fatten with profit to the man who raises it.
Why does he then support a government which says it is good policy to import these into Canada and fatten them here ?
Because he may import something that it is profitable for him to fatten, and export something that is unprofitable for him to try to fatten.

This is a very serious matter so far as the county I represent is concerned. For the year 1902, which is the latest year for which I can get statistics- and these I take from the public documents of Ontario-we sold or slaughtered 20,782 head of cattle valued at $727,370, or $35 per head ? Now the location of my county is similar to that of the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) we live between Detroit and the Niagara rivers. Trainload after trainload of American cattle pass through his city and mine. That is of rather serious consequence to the farmers of our section.
These are cattle in transit from the western to the eastern states.
Certainly.

And if they did not pass through the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Ingram's) county and mine they would be switched off at Toledo and go south of Lake Erie to Buffalo, passing entirely through United States territory. The shorter route is through Canada.
I agree with the hon. gentleman's statement, but I do not quite see the object of his interruption.

I did not mean to interrupt the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram). I may not have caught exactly what he said. But I understood him to speak of trainloads of cattle passing through my county and his, and I thought the facts that I have mentioned important in that connection.

I have not arrived at the point where the interruption would come in. But I shall reach that point soon. I was going to point out that the Americans would Mr. BLAIN.
have an unfair advantage over our cattle growers in connection with this trade, if the duty were one sided, for it would be a simple matter for them to drop off certain of these carloads of cattle to compete in our markets with our cattle.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) knows better than that.

Let us see. Suppose that this government were to reduce duty from twenty per cent to ten per cent while the Americans, instead of leaving their duty at twenty-seven per cent, were to raise it to thirty-five.
Say forty.

I want to accommodate my hon. friend, so, let it go at forty. Under these circumstances does he not think the Americans would have a great advantage with these trainloads of cattle passing through our country ?
Not a bit.

Of course, I cannot see it' through the same spectacles as my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan). But I know that the people of Elgin regard this as a very serious matter. Let me give the hon. gentleman an instance of what may be seen in the small cities of New York state, and that might reasonably occur in the cities of Ontario. Let my hon. friend, some Saturday, drop down to Ogdensburg and, before entering the city, let him pass through eight or ten miles of country on the American side and talk with the farmers there as he has opportunity and find out how many cattle the farmers in that neighbourhood are raising and compare the number with the number of cattle in the neighbourhood of Windsor where he lives. Then let him go to Ogdensburg and find the condition of the meat trade there. He will find butchers there carrying on business as everywhere else. But he will not find them buying from the farmers in the neighbourhood of Ogdensburg to any great extent. And Why? Because the big meat industries of Chicago send in their frozen meat into Ogdensburg and suppply the butchers directly. The moment a butcher tries to buy stock from the farmers about Ogdensburg he is closed up because he cannot compete with the frozen meat imported from the great operators in Chicago. If hon. gentlemen opposite remove the duty, we shall be reduced to the level of the United States in this respect and the conditions that we find about Ogdensburg will exist about St. Thomas or Windsor. Now, in the matter of corn-
We are talking about meat.
I know the hon. gentleman does not want to hear about corn.
On the contrary, I am most anxious.
The hon. gentleman is in favour of a duty on corn.
I am in favour of the policy of the present government.
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of the removal of the duty ?
The duty was removed from corn so far as our cattle feeders were concerned, but not so far as the distillers were concerned.
Did the hon. gentleman approve of the removal of that duty ?
Most decidedly. I voted for it.
I am glad to hear the hon. gentleman state that. He is more outspoken than the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell).

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to prolong this discussion, but it seems necessary to say a word or two. My hon. friend from Bast Elgin (Mr. Ingram) closed on the question of corn. The people of my district,-the people of the counties of Essex and Kent and extending into West Lambton and West Elgin are the largest corn producers in the Dominion of Canada. Under the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power, if a man wanted to import'corn for the distillers, to be made Into Canadian whisky and in that form to be exported, he got it free of duty or, at least he got a rebate of 90 per cent-
Ninety-nine.

I was not exactly sure of the figures, and I wanted to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) the benefit of any doubt. He shook his head at ninety, will he shake his head at ninety-nine ? I want to put this fairly. If a Canadian distiller wanted to import Canadian corn to make Canadian whisky and export to the United States for the Yankee to drink, he got ninety-nine per cent of a rebate on the duty he paid on the corn. But if a Canadian cattle grower, a Canadian farmer, wanted to import American corn to fatten Canadian cattle to ship to the British markets he had to pay the duty and he got no rebate. This government came in and they said : That is unfair to the man who fattens Canadian cattle and at the same time it gives an undue preference to the man who makes Canadian whisky. They say that if a man wants to import American corn to fatten Canadian cattle for the British market he shall stand upon the same basis as the Canadian distiller. And that is why my hon. friend rose in his place to-night as the champion of the Canadian distiller for the purpose of manufacturing whisky for the American drinker instead of supplying the British consumer who wants to eat Canadian beef fattened upon American corn.
The hon. gentleman speaks about Ogdens-burg and Chicago. Do I understand the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) to say that a farmer w'ho fattens a bullock near Ogdensburg has to kill it or ship it to the city of Chicago to be killed, and then ship it all the way back to Ogdensburg in order to sell it to the consumer in Ogdensburg ?
Does the hon. gentleman want an answer now ?
Most decidedly, I would like to hear an answer to that.

I gave the hon. gentleman credit for more sense than to make such a statement. I have always advocated, as a protectionist-and I believe no protectionist does otherwise-that the nearer you get your farmer to the market the better it is for him. I never supposed that a farmer would fatten stock at Ogdensburg and send it to Chicago to be killed and then bring it back again. If that is the hon. gentleman's idea of trade matters, then I should not think he would be very hard to answer. While I am on my feet, as the hon. gentleman is dealing with corn

	-

No, I am not asking about corn ; I was speaking of bullocks-I stick to that word-and I understood the hon. member for East Elgin to plead that because the farmers near Ogdensburg were overcome by competition with meat from the city of Chicago
No.
Every man who heard him understood that was his argument.

I will speak again for my hon. friend's advantage ; he is not very clear. What I said was that the difference between the neighbourhood of Windsor and the neighbourhood of Ogdensburg must be considered. In the neighbourhood of Ogdensburg the farmers do not raise cattle to the extent they do near the city of Windsor, for the reason that the former do not find a favourable home market at Ogdensburg. Why ? Because the frozen meat brought into Ogdensburg from Chicago by cold storage gives them such an unfair competition that they cannot compete with it.

Now I think I understand the hon. gentleman. He means that the farmers near Ogdensburg do not find as ready a market for their beef as the farmers near"the city of Windsor, on account of competition from the city of Chicago, which drives the people of Ogdensburg from the home market What better argument then does my hon. friend want for the farmers of the county of Essex, when he considers that the city of Windsor, or the county of Essex, lies 400 miles nearer to Chicago than the city of Ogdensburg ? Whatever the reason may be, whether it is duty or no duty, granting that it is the duty, then do I find that my

lion, friend is complaining against this government for preserving the duty ?
Not at all ; 1 am finding fault because they do not increase it.

Why do Jou want to increase it when there is no complaint from the county of Essex, which lies 400 miles nearer Chicago than Ogdensburg, and when there is a complaint from the state of New York, where the higher duty prevails and not from the county of Essex ? I want to tell my hon. friend that seven years have come and gone since the wiser policy was inaugurated. Let me tell my hon. friend from East Elgin that if he will go into the matter of the shipments of cattle and meats from the United States into Canada, or of farm products from Canada into the United States, he will find by the statistics of the two countries that every farmer in the Dominion of Canada sells $5 worth to the Americans for every ifl that an American sells to Canadians in farm produce.
What kind of farm produce ?

All kinds. I will tell the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), who is now looking up the statistics, that last night I listened to him, and I listened to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), when they were discussing the question of market-garden produce ; and if he will take farm produce, he will find that every Canadian in the Dominion of Canada sells $5 worth to the Americans for every $1 that an American sells to the Canadians. Now,
I do not want to be misunderstood, Mr. Chairman; I do not want to go upon the record as saying that that is a fair comparison.
Oh, oh.

True; but I do not want the hon. gentleman to fall into the error that Mr. Watson Griflin fell into in St. John. When you are quoting exact figures and exact percentages, remember that you are dealing with a nation of five and a half millions alongside a nation of eighty millions. When you start out by dealing with the percentage of purchases from the 80,000,000 of the United States instead of with sales from the Canadian people to the 80,000,000, then you fall into the same error in argument that I am to-night apologizing to the committee for advancing. It is an unfair comparison; but if it is fair for you to indulge in percentage of purchases, it is equally fair for me to indulge in percentage of sales. I will go a step further, and I tell the hon. member for Peel that he can place the population of the Dominion of Canada at 6,000,000 and of the United States at 75,000,000, and he will find that every Canadian in the Dominion of Canada sells to the American republic ?5 worth of merchandise for every ?1 worth of merchandise that every American sells to the Canadian.

I go one step further, and I tell him that when he comes down to the question of farm produce-yes, Mr. Chairman, and he can include in that bananas-yes, he can include pine-apples, and lastly, he can go to the high ideal of politics of hon. gentlemen opposite, and he can include peanuts -put that in the category also, and I tell him that every Canadian in the Dominion of Canada sells $4 worth of farm produce, even including pine-apples, bananas and peanuts, to the American people for every $1 worth that they sell to Canadians. And the sooner hon. gentlemen opposite get out of their swaddling clothes and realize that one Canadian can get a better meal off sixteen people in the United States than sixteen people can get off one Canadian, the better it will be for the hon. gentlemen opposite.
Mr. Chairman, I thought a circus was going on in some other part of the city, but it appears a portion of it is left in the House of Commons for us to deal with.
That is since the hon. gentleman rose to his feet.

The question of farm products is the question under consideration. My hon. friend has made a very sweeping statement but has given no facts to the committee. May I be permitted to ask the hon. gentleman to name one article of farm products we export to the United States more than we import ? Would the hon. gentleman say one ?
Yes.
Does the hon. gentleman say we export more than we import of farm products?
If the hon. gentleman wants to know what we import I say bananas, peanuts, oranges, pineapples.

The hon. gentleman cannot play anything but the clown. We are not responsible for that and I am sure the hon. Minister of Agriculture will not feel grateful to the hon. gentleman for interrupting his estimates in this way. My hon. friend made the statement a few moments ago that we exported more farm products to the United States than we imported.
No, no ; pardon me.
Yes, yes ; none of your nonsense. My hon. friend made that statement.
No. I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman for Peel does not want to be unfair. He may have misunderstood me.
I could not misunderstand the statement of the hon. gentleman, but I will give him an opportunity to make it again.

The hon. gentleman must see the unfairness and fallacy of comparing two nations, one of seventy-live million or eighty million and the other with less than six million, on the question of percentage of purchases. Percentage of sales would show on the other hand an equally fair statement for the other side. I did not say we export to the United States of any article a greater quantity or value than we import. We may but I am not prepared to say we do.
You said so here.

No, no. If my hon. friend will listen to me I will explain. If my hon. friend will base his statement on seventy-five millions of Americans and five and a half millions of Canadians he will find that every Canadian sold five dollars worth to an American for every one dollar's worth that an American sold to a Canadian.
I cannot understand the the hon. gentleman's explanation. It is entirely different from his former statement to the committee.
No.
My hon. friend says ' no.' Surely my hon. friend has not been listening-

Will my hon. friend from Peel pardon me for a moment ? I will give him the exact figures as I have them. We sold to the Americans $50,000,000 worth of merchandise. That is, each Canadian sold $8.25 worth. They sold to us $128,000,000 worth or $1.60 for every American. In other words every Canadian sold to an American $6 worth for every $1 worth that an American sold to a Canadian.
What sort of an argument is that ?
If my hon. friend from Prince West (Mr. Hackett) will allow me
That is rot.
Just allow the hon. member for Essex to proceed.
Then our sales of farm produce amount to $8,000,000. That is $1.33 per head of the population of Canada.
Not bullocks.

My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) cannot get the word ' bullock ' out of his mind. I am sorry I mentioned it. In fact I am sorry I did not mention cows because that would not have disturbed the hon. member for Montmorency. To go back to farm produce we sold over $8,000,000 worth and on the basis of six millions of a population that is $1.33 per head of the Canadian population. The Americans sold to us of farm produce $17,-
400,000, or call it seventeen and a half millions worth. That means 214 cents worth that every Yankee sold to a Canadian as against $1.33 worth that every Canadian sold to an American. Therefore, it justifies my expression that I thought six million Canadians could get a better meal off seventy-five million Yankees than seventy-five million Yankees could get off six million Canadians.
I do not wish to follow those strange utterances of the hon. gentleman. I may say to hon. gentlemen opposite that I would not wish to make an exhibition of myself like that.
I hope that is not a reflection.

As soon as my hon. friend gets quieted down we will proceed with the question under discussion. We were discussing the question of farm produce imported into Canada and exported from Canada to the United States. I asked the hon. gentleman a simple question and he has been unable to answer it. He made the sweeping statement that we exported more farm products to the United States than we imported, and when I ask him to give one fact in support of that statement he could not do so.
Me ?
Yes.

Not at all. I pulled from my pocket a paper and from that paper I gave the hon. gentleman the figures. I can very readily understand, that, after reading the speech of Watson Griffin, it is very difficult for my hon. friend to understand it. What I said was that we exported eight million dollars worth of farm produce and imported $17,400,000 worth.
Pardon me.

Will my hon. friend pardon me when I tell him that six million people sold to the United States $8,000,000 worth of farm products and that the United States with a population between seventy-five million and eighty million, fifteen times our population, only sold to us $17,400,000 worth. I hope I will not be misunderstood now when I tell the hon. gentleman that every Canadian sold to an American $1.33 worth of farm produce while each citizen of the United States sold to us 214 cents worth; in other words that every Canadian in the Dominion sold to the United States $6 worth of farm produce for every $1 worth of farm produce that an American sold to a Canadian.
Now that my hon. friend has repeated that four or five times I hope he is satisfied.
And I hope you understand it by this time.
Surely my hon. friend does not want me to understand the figures that were handed to him by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) because he does not understand them himselt.
No, these are my own. These others are the figures of my hon. friend from Brant. The figures of my hon. friend from Brant are down here.
Perhaps that is a better explanation of why they are not good authority.
I have these in my inside pocket.

I think my hon. friend must have brought them in his pocket, but leaving that question aside my hon. friend was fasting some reflection upon the remarks I addressed to the House last night upon the trade between Canada and the United States in respect to farm products.

No, I supposed you were dealing with purchases instead of sales. No man is fairer than the hon. member for Peel ; I cast no reflection on him ; I did not challenge the figures he quoted. But I did blame him that he was dealing with purchases instead of sales. I dealt with sales. I do not say it is a fair comparison, but I do say that it is as fair an argument as for the hon. gentleman to deal with purchases.

For the information of my hon. friend, let me point out that last year, 1903, we imported from the United States butter to the value of 8137,054 ; cheese to the value of 830,401 : eggs to the value of $121,262, or $289,317 worth of these three farm products. Now, we exported to the United States last year, butter to the value of $10,225 ; cheese to the value of $7,779 ; eggs to the value of $6,436, or a total of $24,440 that we export to the United States ; as against $289,317 that we imported from the United States, or a balance of $264,877 against us. Does the member for Essex think that is fair to our farmers.
Multiply that by fifteen and see where you land.

That is simply drawing a red herring across the track. Is it fair that the American farmer can send his pork to Canada paying a duty of two cents per pound, while the Canadian farmer will have to pay a duty of five cents per pound to send his pork to the United States ?
I do not think it is fair to discuss the tariff in this committee. Perhaps it would be better for us to get back to the item.
I did not introduce the discussion. I agree with the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion further, but I have to point out
I had intended to call the attention of the House to the fact that we have travelled a long way from the original question, and we had better perhaps get back to it,
If you had done that a little sooner it would have been better. The first to raise the question was the minister himself, and if you stopped it then you would not have had the scene you had to-night.
I know that my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) does not want to misrepresent what I have said. He stated that I was in favour of free corn for the distillers-
I made no such statement.
I trust the hon. member. (Mr. Cowan) will not press the discussion on this point.
I ask the permission of the hon. member for East Elgin to .explain, and if the chair says we are both out of order, I have nothing to say.

This question can come up for discussion with greater appropriateness on another occasion. I thought it only fair to allow the member for Peel to answer the statement of the hon. member for Essex. The discussion should end there.
The member for Essex accused me of supporting a government that was in favour of free corn for the distillers of this country.
I did not.
Then I am glad you didn't.

I said that the hon. gentleman supported a government which gave the distillers 99 per cent of a rebate on corn that they imported from the United States to make whisky of to export back to the United States, while they did not give that rebate to the farmer who imported American corn to feed his cattle and wanted to export the beef back to the United States.
The truth half told is worse than a lie.
I will have to rule that the discussion must cease at this point.
I rise to a personal explanation. It was not the policy of the Conservative government
The hon. gentleman can make a personal explanation so far as the direct charge! against him is concerned, but in doing so he cannot enter into a general statement as to policy.

I am within my rights and I will stand by my rights. I do not nor did I support such a policy as that described by the hon. member (Mr. powan) because there was no such policy in existence. The duty on corn was seven and a half cents against the distiller for all whisky sold in Canada. That is the policy I supported and that is the policy to-day. The starch manufacturer had to pay seven and a half cents on American corn, and if he exported the manufactured article he received a rebate of two and a half cents. I supported a duty upon corn, and why did I do so? Look at the figures and you will see the reason. In 1903 there was imported free of duty 6,033,898 bushels of corn, to compete with the farmers in the corn-growing counties of Kent, Essex and Elgin, and I represent the county of Elgin and the farmers of that county. Does the member for Essex favour the removal of duty on corn, when in his own county they produced 3,603,765 bushels of corn, according to the statistics of the Bureau of Industries, for Ontario, for the year 1902, and that amount of corn is valued at $1,463,129.
Corn was 20 cents per bushel higher after the duty was taken off than it was before.

I think we were discussing something with reference to exhibitions and have rather wandered from the subject. I have had a great afternoon and this evening is a fitting complement to it. I went to the circus before six o'clock and have been at another circus ever since. I looked over the animals down there this afternoon, and while I found some larger animals there which we have not here, I do not think that the monkeys began to compare with the specimens we have in this House ; but coming back to the item under discussion, I understood from the Minister of Agriculture that one of the results which followed the Japan exhibition was a great increase in the export of butter and flour. I would like to ask him if it is really the case that we have increased our exports of butter to Japan as the result of that exhibition ?

I said that we had been exporting butter from the government creamery in Alberta steadily some years back to a small extent, and that since the exhibition that export had increased very materially. I think that we are now exporting about four times as much per month as we did before the exhibition.
Then general exports from Canada ?
I have not examined the trade and navigation returns and cannot tell.

I cannot believe that the hon. minister would intend to deceive this House by claiming results from exhibitions which have not followed them. The expenditure on these exhibitions has been questioned on the ground that it is very doubtful whether we get a good return for our money. In reply to that criticism, the minister told us that since the exhibition we had introduced Canadian flour into Japan and that Canadian flour was unknown there previously. Well, Sir, what do we find ? I find by the official returns that in the year 1900 we sent to that country 2.379 barrels of flour and that we have sent there as high as 3,035 barrels. But last year, 1903. we only sent 611 barrels. Evidently therefore the minister's statement that the exhibition was the cause of the introduction of Canadian flour into Japan was absolutely wrong. Not only was that statement wrong, but the trade, instead of increasing as a consequence of that exhibition, has decreased. Last year, after the exhibition, we only sent one-fifth the quantity of flour which we had sent three years previous. I do not like to say that the hon. gentleman intended wilfully to deceive this House, but the statistics are there, and he has just as free access to them as anybody else ; and when he stands up here and asks us to vote an increase of $50,000 for exhibition purposes, he owes it to his position as a minister, when he at-temps to justify that increase, to justify it on statements which are absolutely correct and not on imaginary facts.
With regard to butter, we have the same condition of things. Five or six years ago, we were shipping more butter to Japan than we did last year. Last year we shipped 8,000 pounds, but we shipped as high as 12,000 pounds three years ago. I am not going to say that these exhibitions do not do good. I hope they do. I think it is well 'that these exhibitions should be held in countries with which we can encourage trade, but I do not think they are of much use in countries with which we are doing less and less trade every year. It may be good policy to have an exhibit in St. Louis, which will show to intending settlers the resources of this country in the shape of minerals, products of the soil and so forth, but I warn the hon. minister, that if he wishes to have the respect of this House, he will see that what information he gives is based on fact and is not misleading.

The hon. gentleman is slightly wrong in his dates, and what he

has said justifies the claim I made. Our exports to Japan of flour a few years ago were rather large, because certain millers sent a large consignment to that country. They sent that shipment as a result of the visit of an agent sent there by my hon. colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce some four or five years ago. Following his visit, there was a considerable shipment of flour to Japan, but it was not advertised, the markets were not prepared for it, it was not a success, and the result was that in the few years following there was hardly any shipment of flour to that country at all.
What few years ?

Ending the 30th of June last. We sent some 3,000 barrels in 19001901. In 1902 and 1903 the shipments decreased. The exhibition in Japan opened in March of 1903 and did not close until August, 1903. after the end of the fiscal year 1903, which the hon. gentleman has quoted, and the results of the exhibition in Japan had no effect whatever on the trade of a year which closed before the close of the exhibition. The result of the exhibition on our trade have been in the fiscal year commencing July 1st, 1903. The figures which I quoted and the statement I made, have been absolutely correct within my own knowledge.
What are the figures?
I gave the figures with regard to the shipments of flour.
Can the minister give any figures in relation to the steady increase in the shipments of flour and similar products from the United States to Japan?

No. I have stated what I know to be the absolute result of our flour and bread making exhibit in Japan. I know of orders placed in Canada to the extent of a considerable number of carloads as a direct result of our exhibit. ,1 stated also that as a result of our exhibit the butter export has increased to something like four times as much per month as formerly. I also stated that other people l'.ad received special orders. I recall a re: quest which came from the Consul General of Japan to put a certain person in \ okohoma into communication with butter makers and producers in Canada as they wish to open a direct trade and to place orders for such butter.
Were any of these purchases made by the Japanese government in consequence of the war ?
Not that I am aware of.

Is the butter produced in Alberta of the best quality we can Mr. FISHER.
*

produce in Canada ? If it is not, should we not send other shipments of the best that we have?

The butter made at the government creameries at Alberta is of very high quality. I shall not say it is of the very best quality in Canada. The butter in Japan was not all from the government creameries:1 That from the government creameries compared favourably with any other butter on the Japanese market, but there was an exhibition of butter from Ontario which was superior to the butter of the Northwest creameries. There were a number of different exhibits there ; and I may say, generally speaking, that our butter compared favourably with any butter that was sent to the Japanese market from other countries.
The hon. minister is changing his position. He told this House that Canadian flour was an unknown quantity.
I said that Canadian flour was unknown on the Japanese market as Canadian flour.

But we had previously shipped Canadian flour as Canadian flour. The minister told us just now that the representative of this government went there five years ago and introduced this trial shipment 5 or 6 years ago. Yet the minister stands up and says that this exhibition was the means of the introduction of Canadian flour into this market when he knew it had been introduced 4 or 5 years ago.

The introduction of 4 or 5 years ago was a failure, and as a result of that failure the shipments were not followed up. When the exhibition took place Canadian flour was unknown as Canadian flour in the Japanese market.
Would the hon. minister explain what kinds of goods were purchased by his government and exhibited at the Japan exhibition ?

The articles sold were, rubber goods, paper and pulp, pulp wood, some products of pulp in the shape of pails and vessels of one kind and another, butter, canned goods, lumber in the shape of shingles, finished lumber and sashes, doors, Ac., some glass goods, furniture, a small exhibit of bicycles and bicycle parts, flour for the making of bread, a small exhibit or ropes and cordage, a few hams and bacon, cooking stoves, oil stoves, tinware, a baking machine and oven. There was some honey and a piano. Those were the sales. A large number of goods were of a perishable character, apples and fuits for instance, which we could not sell. By the time they had been exhibited they were no use. We were asked by the different agricultural colleges of the government in Japan for our exhibits of grain, &c. We

presented them to these Institutions as specimens of Canadian products and charged nothing for them.

At D-24 of the Auditor General's Report, I see an item-
The Canada Furniture Manufacturers, Toronto, oak bureaus, 5 at $18 ; maple bureau, $23
Would the hon. minister say whether these articles were selected as first class products of Canadian makers of furniture, and would he regard this as a proper exhibit of what the Canadian people can do in the way of manufacturing furniture ?

No, they were selected as furniture likely to be suitable to the demands of the Japanese market. We could not sell the highest class there at all. We bought such furniture as would be suitable to that purpose. The items my hon. friend mentions came to $103 and as a matter of fact we sold there furniture to the extent of $568.
Just those items?
I cannot say there was nothing else but that was the chief item. It may possibly have included the school desks which were sent over. I do not see any sale of school desks here.

Would it not be possible when the hon. minister makes an exhibit at a place such as the Japan exhibition to get the Canadian manufacturers themselves to supply these goods, if the government pay the cost of freight, care of the exhibit, Ac.

We tried to get the Canadian furniture manufacturers to do that, but failed. At Buffalo, the year before, this very association supplied us with furniture for our Canadian building and took it back after the exhibition, we paying some slight wear and tear. We tried to get them to do the same in the Osaka exhibition, but they said that Japan was so far away and the market so uncertain that they did not care to do it. Except flour, there was no part of our exhibit in Japan in which there was a better opening than in furniture. We had demands for it the moment it was shown, and could have sold it all within a week after the opening of the .exhibition. But we kept it there and sold it at the end. The articles were sold to high officials such as the minister of agriculture, the prime minister, one of the prince's and so on. They thought so much of the furniture that they were eager purchasers. They had not seen anything to equal it. I have urged upon the Manufacturers' Association to send an agent to Japan to take advantage of the opportunities opened up by the exhibition, for I felt sure that they could immediately work up a very large trade. But they have not
done so simply on the plea that their orders are so great that they cannot fill them and they have no time to attend to this foreign market.
The minister has been badly informed as to the state of the furniture trade in Canada.

I am glad that Canadian furniture is so favourably regarded in the Japanese market. Judging from the sale of rubber goods from that exhibition there should be a good market for these. I understood him to say that the rubber goods were sold for $400, and according to the Blue-book I find that they only cost the country $220.
Of course, we added the freight charges which would be heavy on such goods.
But they would not be $200.
What is the hon. minister's explanation of this sale of rubber goods that cost the country $200 for $400.
That is the figure in the statement furnished me by the officers in the department.
And does the hon. minister credit it ?
Yes.
The hon. minister does not believe it is the same as the statement about the flour ?
Yes. The statement about the flour was correct.

I am sure the minister is wrong when he says the freight on rubber goods would be high. You could hardly find goods that would pack closer and be less expensive.
MrJ FISHER. The figures I have given from this list should be divided by two. These statements are in yen, the Japanese dollar, and not in the Canadian dollar. I did not notice the mark when I read the figures. The price at which the rubber goods sold would be $200, not $400.
When the hon. gentleman speaks of Japan being a splendid field for our furniture, I suppose he includes chairs. Did he educate the people there to sit on chairs ?

I did not need to do so. There are in Japan a large number of people, especially in government and other offices, who use chairs. Desks are also in demand,. One <of the things that they most required was the roll-top desk. My hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) knows a great deal about Japan, but he may not

be hware that In the houses of well-to-do Japanese there are quite commonly one or two rooms furnished in European style, partly for convenience of strangers and partly because there are many Japanese who have lived in Europe or America and who, when they return home prefer to live, to a certain extent at any rate, in European style.
Mr. BLA1N. The explanation the minister gave as to the money would apply in the case of furniture. What, then, was the furniture sold for ?
Half of what I said. Instead of $658, it was 658 yen, or $329.
So this furniture cost $403.07, and was sold at a loss even without allowing anything for freight rates ? Does he then, regard the market for furniture as so very hopeful 7
Do I understand that this item covers the exhibition at Winnipeg 7
No, that is covered by a special item which we passed some weeks ago.

I understood the minister to say that we were not sending any live stock down to St. Louis. I wonder if that accounts for the items I see in connection with the St. Louis exhibition. Here is an item for Shorthorn bull head, $25, and one for a Hereford bull head, $41.88. Are we sending these bulls' heads in order that the visitors to the St. Louis exhibition may know that we do breed cattle in this country 7 And, if that is the object why should we have selected the bull's head. Why not take down the whole bull, or the more essential parts of the bull. I think it would have been better to send down the whole bull than the bull's head. This bull, I think, would be pretty dear. I do not know what the price of a bull would be on the basis of $41.88 for the head, and why should we pay more for a Hereford bull's head than for a Shorthorn bull's head 7 And what is the prejudice against other breeds 7 If we are to have an exhibit of bulls' heads, why not include the Jersey, the Guernsey, the Holstein and other breeds so that there may be no favouritism 7 The breeder of Shorthorns in this country may feel pleased to know that the bull's head has gone down. But he would be better satisfied if the whole bull had gone.
I am not up in scientiflc agriculture as the hon. gentleman is, but there may be some reason why he bought this head and sent it down there. Now, so far as the other breeds are concerned, I think the discrepancy in the price of this Hereford head will cause trouble, because it is not going to be pleasant to the Durham men or the Shorthorn breeders to know that a greater value is placed upon the Hereford than upon other Mr. FISHER.
breeds. Then there is the Jersey man with no bull there at all, what is he going to do 7 And the Guernsey man, the Galloway man, the Polled-Angus man, the Holstein man- none of these men, with whom these breed! are favourites, will have any bulls representing them, or any bulls' heads representing them at this exhibition. I would call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that his department is liable to become unpopular if he selects out a head here and a head there, and leaves all these other important breeds unrepresented-and deadheads, as an hon. friend near me suggests.
I would suggest that the minister take into consideration whether it would not be better to send the whole bull properly equipped down to St. Louis, one that would do full credit to the breed he is supposed to represent. The hon. gentleman might make some arrangement with the government at Washington. If there is any difficulty about [DOT] getting them into that country, he pught to be able to make some special arrangement -perhaps not for the cows or the heifers, but for bulls, a real genuine, complete bull of each of the several breeds. I would suggest that the minister take this into his careful consideration, because I think it is unfair that he should only send the heads of two bulls down there and leave the other breeds unrepresented.
I would just say .to the hon. gentleman that these heads he speaks of were bought for decorative purposes in the agricultural exhibit there.

That may be ; but I do not think it would look proper to practical farmers-we should all try to be practical farmers -that the head of the bull is the essential decoration of the bull. I do not think we should look upon it in that light. I think we should send the animal complete in every respect.

I understood the minister to say that he had received communications from the Breeders' Association of Canada with regard to sending live stock to the St. Louis exhibition, and that lie now has the subject under consideration.
I explained that a few minutes ago.

The Breeders' Association hold the best stock in the Dominion, and unless the United States government will allow them to go in there and make a good show, I am afraid that the reputation of Canadian stock will suffer. I do not think it would be wise for a few individual farmers to send in stock that is not of the highest character, as Canadian stock would be belittled in the eyes of foreigners who go there.

Under the arrangement we propose only first-class animals will be likely to go, as it will be only in case they

get good prizes that they will receive assistance.
I do not think that we can get a good exhibition of our stock there if individuals have to take cattle at their own expense and run all risk. I fear the best cattle of Canada will not he there.
Could the minister give the total amount that was paid for goods for the Japan exhibition, and the amount leceived for the sale of those goods at that exhibition ?

I could not give the total amount paid, because it is involved in a lot of small items which I have not added up yet. The total amount received was in the neighbourhood of $10,000, but the total amount paid was a good deal more than that.
I understood the minister to say that the total amount paid on account of that exhibition was over $60,000, but he has only received $10,000 back. Does the former amount include salaries ?

Yes ; salaries, cost of installation, freight on goods and all preparations for the exhibition. 1 -would point out also that many of these goods were perishable. We had to buy a large amount of fruit, for instance.

I would ask the minister again about the question of furniture. No doubt his remarks will be carefully read by the manufacturers of furniture in this country. Now, the minister said that there was a good market in Japan for furniture. I would like to know how he thinks he would be encouraging furniture manufacturers to ship goods to Japan in face of the fact stated by him that he paid $400 for furniture and paid freight on it, and only received about $300 for it after he was through with it. In other words, are we to understand that the commissioners were not able to dispose of these goods at their actual cost ? No doubt he got them at a very low price.
The regular market price.

Together with freight added. The commissioner was not able to get more than about 50 per cent on the dollar, because $400 worth of goods, together with the freight, would probably be $600, and the minister says he only got something like about $300. The hon. minister stated that they got a sum of about $300. I suppose the hon. minister feels that the commissioner did his duty while there, and got the actual market value for these goods. If so, he must admit that the amount received was only about 50 cents on the dollar, so that the manufacturers of furniture would not receive more than 50 cents on the dollar upon the amount they charged the government. How does the hon minster make out 132
that that was encouraging the manufacturers to ship goods to that country ?

I may say that I based my statements inr regard to the market that we have there for furniture on the actual prices that are charged there for European and American furniture. Individuals in Japan came and asked what this furniture could be laid down there for and they said that they had paid larger prices for inferior goods. We had to sell the goods that had been there on exhibition during the whole summer and I daresay that my commissioners were not able to get the first hand price for any of them. I know as a matter of fact that some of these goods were sold very low to people of importance in whose hands we wanted to place them for advertising purposes, and I am not quite certain but that some of it was even given away for that purpose. The total of this amount was the actual cash received but I would not for a moment allow it to be held that these prices were the total value of these goods had they been placed first hand on the market or had they been offered in the ordinary market.
I have had a little experience myself in regard to goods at exhibitions and I have always found that goods that have been made specially for an exhibition are a little better that the ordinary goods.
These goods were not; they were just ordinary trade goods.

We generally get a little higher price. The government had that exhibition in Japan for the purpose of encouraging trade and the hon. minister says now that he has found out from the manufacturers of furniture that there is a good market in Japan. He has worked it up for them, and he has said to them : If you will send your goods there you will get a good market at paying prices. Will the hon. minister assume the responsibility of allowing any manufacturing industry to send a consignment of goods to Japan and guarantee that they will bring the actual cost of production in this country ?

No, that would not be the government's work. The government would not undertake to do that. The country would not ask the government to do that and the House would not support the government in doing that. The point is that by the exhibition of Canadian goods we showed to the people of Japan the character and quality of the goods that can be produced in this country. We must then trust to the ordinary channels of trade to follow that up, and it is only if the ordinary channels of trade will follow it up that the trade can be established.
Have tliere been any shipments made since that exhibition ?

The furniture association have not taken the steps we asked them to take:	When Mr. Hutchison, the commissioner, and Mr. Burns, the secretary of our exhibition there talked matters over with them they said that they were so busy with their work here that they did not care to undertake shipments to Japan at the present time.

If I understood the hon. minister correctly at the outset he made a statement to the committee in regard to four 1 or five exhibitions. Would the hon. gentleman say how much he expects the total cost of the St. Louis exhibition to be and how much the probable cost of the other exhibitions that he mentioned will be ?

This is an item of $200,000 which I am asking now for next year.
I am expecting to apply about $125,000 of this to closing up the accounts in connection with the St. Louis exhibition. That will leave about $75,000. When I asked for that item I was discussing the question of an exhibition in South Africa. Since then I have received information of the organization which has led me to believe that it is not of a character that we ought officially to take part in. But, I have also officially on behalf of the government, accepted an invitation to take part in the universal exhibition at Liege which is to open on the 1st of May next year.
About how much do you expect to expend there ?
About $50,000, somewhere in the neighbourhood of the amount we expended at Osaka,-possibly not so much as Lifige is a little more accessible than Osaka.
What will be the total cost of the St. Louis exhibition ?
And those others ?
I want to have about $25,000 available so as to be in a position to take part in these other exhibitions which 1 have mentioned.

Has the hon. Minister of Agriculture ever looked at the question in this way ? There is an expenditure of $325,000 on the St. Louis exhibition. I had the honour of being the only member of the House of Commons who voted against the payment of a large sum towards the expense of making an exhibition at the World's Fair. Would it not be better to take that sum of money and spend it on Immigration ? If the hon. minister would take that $325,000 and apply it to immigration it would bring out to Canada several Mr. FISHER.
thousand immigrants. I should imagine that it would bring out about 10,000 people. Does not the hon. minister think that that sum of money expended in bringing 10,000 selected immigrants to the shores of Canada would be infinitely better employed than if it were spent in this flimflamming around St. Louis and other places ? I think the money should be voted to the Department of the Interior. My own personal opinion is that these exhibitions do not do the country one particle of good.
I do not agree with the hon. gentleman.
And I am of opinion that if the money were expended in the other way which I have suggested, better results would "be achieved.

I am very glad that my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) has brought that question up because it is one which has influenced my colleagues and myself in regard to these exhibtions at St. Louis and Liege. We are getting a very considerable number of Americans from the western part of the Union.
Through the energy of the Interior Department ?

Through the energy of the Interior Department. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (air. Sifton) quite coincided with me as to the advisability for immigration purposes of having a representative exhibit in agriculture, forestry and mineral resources at St. Louis. Mr. Hutcheson was at St. Louis three or four weeks before the exhibition opened and during that time he was besieged with inquiries as to the opportunities of the Northwest for immigration purposes. In our building at St. Louis my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has a staff of immigration agents who are distributing literature and imparting information in regard to the Northwest. I had quoted to me tonight by a gentleman who was at St. Louis a little while ago with the press party there an incident which illustrates the effect that our exhibit at St. Louis is having. He said : I was talking with a gentleman, an editor, from Kansas and he said to me that he had never been able to understand how it was that their best citizens were leaving the United States and going to Canada but since he had seen the Canadian exhibit at St. Louis he did not wonder at it because we showed up there magnificently in comparison with their own western states. I have seen already, and I dare say1 hon. gentlemen opposite have seen, references made to the Canadian exhibition at St. Louis, and it is declared that the exhibition is not only creditable to Canada but that it is an eye-opener and surprise to the people of the western states and I venture to think it will be one of the strongest inducements for immigra-

tion into the Northwest and I am glad to .get this endorsement from my hon. friend of this expenditure.
Tracadie lazaretto, $5,500.
Are the lepers increasing or decreasing ?

There are always in the neighbourhood of twenty or twenty-five.
Public Works Health Act, $3,000.
What is the cause of the decrease 1

Last year I asked for $4,000, and we did not spend $3,000 ; but I warn my hon. friends that when I made the decrease I had not realized the necessity of the construction of the new t*ancontinental railway, and in my suppplementary estimates, I am afraid I will not only have to restore the decrease, but to ask for a couple of thousand more. I think it very necessary that on the construction of the new transcontinental railway, we should take special precautions to avoid such difficulties as arose on the Grows' Nest Pass.
Did the minister expect that the Transcontinental Railway Bill would be defeated in the House ?

No. But to tell the truth I didn't think of it when I made up this
item. Notwithstanding that we have not passed a great many items, I feel that consideration is due to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I shall move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again
Some resolutions reported.
What business to-morrow ?
I think we will proceed with the quarantine estimates and perhaps the estimates of the Minister of Marine. We will proceed with some Bills first.
Will you go on with the Militia Bill ?

No, and as the Minister of Justice is not here we will not proceed with liis Bills.
